docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
PyDataUI is a modern full-stack web, mobile, and desktop framework designed for Data Engineers, Data Analysts, AI/ML Engineers, and Python developers. It bridges the gap between toy prototype libraries (Streamlit, Gradio) and complex multi-language web stacks (React + TypeScript + FastAPI).

With PyDataUI: - 🐍 100% Python Code: Build responsive web, mobile (Android/iOS), and desktop apps without writing JavaScript, Swift, or Kotlin. - ⚡ FastAPI Default Engine: Native ASGI foundation running on standard FastAPI and Uvicorn with zero C/Rust compilation requirements. - 🦀 Optional PyRustAPI Core: Seamlessly switch to an ultra-high-throughput compiled Rust HTTP engine (Tokio & Hyper) delivering up to 34,000+ req/sec for hyper-scale workloads. - 🔌 Native FastAPI Mounting: Mount PyDataUI dashboards, admin consoles, and AI tools directly inside existing FastAPI backends via mount(api, app, path="/dashboard"). - 🪄 Dual Developer Experience: Use the rapid procedural API (import pydataui as ui; ui.title(...); ui.run()) for instant scripts, or the declarative Component & State system for large-scale enterprise applications. - 📱 Cross-Platform Mobile & Desktop: Built-in Progressive Web App (PWA), Capacitor mobile shell (Android .apk and iOS .ipa), and standalone desktop apps (--desktop or Tauri 2.0). - 🎨 Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui: Modern design system with dark mode, CSS variables, and accessible components. - ⚡ Reactive SSR via HTMX: State changes trigger hypermedia fragment responses that update the DOM dynamically without client-side virtual DOM overhead. - 🤖 AI & Agent Ready: Built-in Chat, Markdown, and CodeEditor components compatible with LangGraph, UnifiedNexus, and LLMs. - 🔒 Auth & API Keys: Built-in JWT authentication, RBAC (@require_auth(roles=[...])), and secure API keys (pdu_live_...). - 📊 Enterprise Page Templates: Pre-packaged analyst, data quality, pipeline, and ML model registry templates via pydataui.templates. - 🌐 One-Click Sharing (share=True): Create public internet tunnels instantly via Cloudflare or ngrok for remote client demos. - 📖 Automatic REST APIs: Every reactive State class automatically creates OpenAPI-documented REST endpoints for external data integration.

docs.title: 4. Installation & Requirements
docs.text:
PyDataUI requires Python 3.9+.

# Core framework
pip install pydataui

# With data science & ML dependencies (pandas, plotly, pyarrow)
pip install "pydataui[data]"

# Full installation (data + tunnel + dev)
pip install "pydataui[all]"

docs.title: 5. Quick Start
docs.text:
Create an app file app.py:

from pydataui import App, State
from pydataui.components import Container, Card, Flex, Button, Heading, Divider

class CounterState(State):
    count: int = 0
    def increment(self): self.count += 1
    def decrement(self): self.count -= 1
    def reset(self): self.count = 0

app = App(title="PyDataUI Counter")

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Container(
        Card(
            title="Reactive Counter",
            children=[
                Flex(
                    Button("-", on_click=CounterState.decrement, variant="danger"),
                    Heading(CounterState.count, level=2),
                    Button("+", on_click=CounterState.increment, variant="success"),
                    align="center", justify="center", gap="lg",
                ),
                Divider(),
                Button("Reset", on_click=CounterState.reset, variant="outline", full_width=True),
            ]
        ),
        max_width="md",
        padding="lg",
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

Run with the CLI: 

pydataui dev app.py --reload

docs.title: Reactive State & StateVar
docs.text:
State in PyDataUI is defined by subclassing State. Typed class variables become reactive state descriptors:

from pydataui import State

class PipelineState(State):
    batch_size: int = 5000
    is_running: bool = False
    status_log: list = []

    def start_pipeline(self):
        self.is_running = True
        self.status_log.append("Started batch run")

    def stop_pipeline(self):
        self.is_running = False
        self.status_log.append("Halted by operator")
  • When referenced at the class level (e.g. PipelineState.batch_size), it returns a StateVarRef which binds to the current user's session snapshot during rendering.
  • When accessed inside a method (self.batch_size), it operates as a standard Python attribute.

docs.title: Event Handlers & SSR
docs.text:
Buttons, forms, and inputs connect to State methods using props:

# Direct method reference
Button("Start", on_click=PipelineState.start_pipeline)

# Lambda with argument capture
Button("Delete", on_click=lambda id=item.id: TableState.delete_item(id))

# Two-way input binding

docs.title: Automatic REST APIs
docs.text:
For every registered State, PyDataUI creates endpoints automatically:

Method Endpoint Description GET /api/{State} Full state dictionary serialized to JSON GET /api/{State}/{field} Single field value PUT /api/{State} Update state variables from JSON body DELETE /api/{State} Reset state instance to class defaults POST /api/{State}/{method} Execute a method (accepts optional JSON payload)

Catalog all states and endpoints: 

curl http://localhost:8000/api

Interactive Swagger UI: - http://localhost:8000/docs - http://localhost:8000/api/docs

docs.title: Native FastAPI Mounting & Conflict Handling
docs.text:
You can mount any PyDataUI application directly into an existing FastAPI application with a single line of code:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydataui import App, mount

api = FastAPI(title="Production API")
dashboard = App(title="Internal Dashboard")

@dashboard.page("/")
def home():
    return "Operations Control Center"

mount(api, dashboard, path="/dashboard")
# or: dashboard.mount_to(api, path="/dashboard")

docs.title: How PyDataUI Resolves & Prevents Conflicts:
docs.text:
• Route Collisions: Parent FastAPI routes (e.g. /users) and PyDataUI routes (e.g. /dashboard/users) live in isolated routing subtrees with zero collisions.
  • OpenAPI / Swagger Separation: Parent API keeps its root /docs; PyDataUI automatically serves its dedicated interactive docs at /dashboard/docs.
  • Static Asset Sandboxing: PyDataUI isolates internal Tailwind CSS & HTMX under /_pdu/static/*, never clashing with parent /static/*.
  • Session & Cookie Isolation: PyDataUI uses a distinct signed cookie (pdu-session). Parent JWT or session cookies are never touched.
  • Multiple Sub-Apps: You can mount multiple distinct PyDataUI apps (/admin, /portal, /analytics) on one FastAPI app with zero state leakage.

📖 Full Architectural Guide: See FastAPI Mounting & Conflicts.

docs.title: 10. Port Forwarding (share=True)
docs.text:
Share your application with remote stakeholders, clients, or team members with a single flag:

app.run(share=True)
Or via CLI: 
pydataui run app.py --share

Tunnels use pyngrok if installed, or fallback to encrypted SSH port-forwarding via serveo.net.

Located in pydataui.app.App. The central orchestrator integrating routing, state snapshots, REST APIs, middleware, and the HTTP server engine.

from pydataui import App, AppConfig

app = App(
    title="Enterprise AI Operations",
    description="Internal control plane for SLM clusters",
    version="1.2.2",
    debug=False,
    secret_key="your-32-byte-production-secret-key-goes-here",
    session_store=None,     # Defaults to SQLite or Memory
    auth_store=None,        # Defaults to SQLite or Memory
    max_request_size=10 * 1024 * 1024  # 10 MB limit

docs.title: app.page(path: str, title: Optional[str] = None, layout: Optional[Callable] = None)
docs.text:
Decorator that registers a Server-Side Rendered (SSR) page route.

  • Parameters:
  • path (str): URL pattern (e.g. '/', '/dashboard', '/model/{model_id}').
  • title (Optional[str]): Custom <title> override for this page.
  • layout (Optional[Callable]): Wrapper layout function receiving the page content component.
  • Handler Return Value: Must return a Component instance (e.g. Container, DashboardLayout, Card) or valid HTML string.
  • Example: 
    @app.page("/clusters")
def cluster_view():
    return Container(Heading("Cluster Status", level=1))

docs.title: app.api(path: str, method: str = 'GET', public: bool = False, roles: tuple = (), **kwargs)
docs.text:
Decorator that registers a high-speed custom REST API endpoint on the underlying engine.

  • Parameters:
  • path (str): REST endpoint path (e.g. '/api/v1/telemetry').
  • method (str): HTTP verb ('GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE').
  • public (bool): If True, bypasses authentication. Default is False.
  • roles (tuple[str]): List of required role names (e.g. (Role.ADMIN,)).
  • Example: 
    @app.api("/api/v1/health", method="GET", public=True)
async def health_check():
    return {"status": "healthy", "uptime_s": 84920}

docs.title: app.setup_auth(auth_manager: AuthManager, allow_registration: bool = False)
docs.text:
Mounts standard /api/auth/* endpoints (/login, /logout, /me, /keys) and binds authentication middleware.

  • Parameters:
  • auth_manager (AuthManager): Initialized authentication manager.
  • allow_registration (bool): If True, enables public /api/auth/register.

docs.title: app.mount(path: str, asgi_app: Any)
docs.text:
Mounts an external ASGI application (such as an existing FastAPI, Starlette, or LangGraph backend) under a sub-path prefix.

  • asgi_app (Any): Valid ASGI-compatible app.

docs.title: app.run(host: str = "127.0.0.1", port: int = 8000, reload: bool = False, workers: int = 1, share: bool = False)

Starts the production or development HTTP server.

  • host (str): IP address to bind to ("127.0.0.1" for local, "0.0.0.0" for all interfaces).

docs.title: 2. State & Reactivity
docs.text: PyDataUI provides two state management models: 1. Procedural State (state()): Zero-class procedural hook ideal for scripts, internal dashboards, and prototypes. 2. Object-Oriented State (class State): Class-based reactive store for multi-model enterprise applications.

docs.title: Procedural State Hook: state(**defaults) -> ProceduralState
docs.text:
from pydataui import state

# 1. Initialize state with default values
s = state(
    counter=0,
    active_node="Node-A",
    messages=[{"role": "assistant", "content": "Welcome!"}],
    loading=False
)

# 2. Register reactive action
@s.action
def increment():
    s.counter += 1

@s.action
async def set_node(node_name: str = "", **kwargs):
    s.active_node = node_name or kwargs.get("node", "Node-A")

docs.title: Methods & Attributes on ProceduralState
docs.text:
• @s.action: Decorator registering a function as an interactive server action callable via HTMX or the TUI.
  • s.<variable_name>:
  • Inside @s.action handlers: Resolves to the active session value and permits direct mutation.
  • Inside @app.page layout declarations: Evaluates to a StateVarRef descriptor that renders reactive bindings.
  • s.to_dict() -> Dict[str, Any]: Returns a JSON-serializable dictionary of current state variables.
  • s.reset(): Resets all values back to the original initial values.

docs.title: Class-Based Reactive State: class State
docs.text:
from pydataui import State, StateVar

class ClusterState(State):
    node_count: int = 8
    region: str = "us-east-1"
    is_busy: bool = False

    def scale_up(self):
        self.node_count += 1

    def scale_down(self):
        if self.node_count > 1:
            self.node_count -= 1

docs.title: Lifecycle & Session Isolation
docs.text:
• Each browser session / cookie receives an independent instance of ClusterState.
  • ClusterState.node_count accessed on the class returns a StateVarRef for declarative component binding.
  • self.node_count accessed inside methods operates on the session's isolated instance.

docs.title: class AuthManager(secret_key, token_expire_hours=24, store=None, enable_throttling=True, ...)
docs.text:
Located in pydataui.auth.AuthManager. Implements production security: - Password hashing with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (600,000 rounds) + unique salt. - Signed JSON Web Tokens (JWT) with HMAC-SHA256. - Brute-force rate limiting and lockout protection. - Scoped API keys with prefix pdu_live_.

from pydataui import AuthManager, Role
from pydataui.storage import SQLiteAuthStore

auth = AuthManager(
    secret_key="your-32-byte-secret-key-at-least-32-bytes-long",
    token_expire_hours=24,
    store=SQLiteAuthStore("auth.db"),
    enable_throttling=True,
    max_login_attempts=5,
    lockout_duration_seconds=300
)

docs.text:
PyDataUI supports swappable session and authentication storage backends:

    MemorySessionStore, SQLiteSessionStore, PostgresSessionStore,

docs.title: sniff_tabular_data(data: Any) -> Tuple[List[Dict[str, Any]], List[str]]
docs.text:
Automatically sniffs, extracts columns, and normalizes tabular data from: - pandas.DataFrame - polars.DataFrame - duckdb.PyRelation - pyarrow.Table - list[pydantic.BaseModel] - list[dict]

import polars as pl
from pydataui import DataTable

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "cluster": ["us-east", "eu-west", "ap-south"],
    "nodes": [12, 8, 16],
    "status": ["HEALTHY", "HEALTHY", "WARNING"]
})

DataTable(
    data=df,
    searchable=True,
    paginated=True,
    page_size=10,
    bordered=True
)

docs.title: Authentication, Authorization & API Keys Guide
docs.text: PyDataUI provides a built-in enterprise authentication system designed for data platforms, analytics portals, and automated ETL pipelines.

docs.title: 1. Core Architecture
docs.text: PyDataUI's auth module (pydataui.auth) supports: - Session & JWT Authentication: Sign in via web form or REST API to obtain signed JWT tokens. - Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Assign roles to users and enforce role permissions on pages and endpoints. - Production API Keys (pdu_live_...): Generate scoped API keys for Airflow, Prefect, Cron jobs, and external data consumers. - Zero Heavy Dependencies: Uses standard library hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac for password hashing and PyJWT for JWT signing.

docs.title: 2. Setup & Configuration
docs.text:
from pydataui import App
from pydataui.auth import AuthManager, Role

app = App(title="Corporate Analytics")
auth = AuthManager(
    secret_key="your-secure-random-secret-key-min-32-chars!",
    token_expire_hours=24
)

# Seed initial users
admin = auth.add_user(
    username="admin",
    password="SuperSecurePassword123!",
    email="admin@company.com",
    roles=[Role.ADMIN, Role.DATA_ENGINEER]
)

analyst = auth.add_user(
    username="jane",
    password="JanePassword456!",
    email="jane@company.com",
    roles=[Role.DATA_ANALYST]
)

# Attach auth routes and handlers to app
app.setup_auth(auth)

Calling app.setup_auth(auth) automatically mounts the following REST endpoints: - POST /api/auth/login → Authenticates credentials, returns { "token": "<jwt>" } - POST /api/auth/logout → Invalidate session - GET /api/auth/me → Returns user profile and assigned roles - POST /api/auth/register → Register new user account - GET /api/auth/keys → List user's active API keys - POST /api/auth/keys → Generate a new API key - DELETE /api/auth/keys/{key_id} → Revoke an API key

docs.title: ⚡ Performance Benchmarks: PyDataUI (PyRustAPI) vs FastAPI (Uvicorn)
docs.text:
This benchmark suite provides a rigorous, head-to-head comparison between PyDataUI (powered by the Rust pyrustapi engine on Tokio/Hyper) and FastAPI (running on uvicorn with uvloop).

All tests measure real HTTP performance over loopback TCP sockets using ApacheBench (ab), evaluating both Real GET (payload serialization) and Real POST (Pydantic model validation and serialization) on a local development machine.

docs.title: Profile A: High-Concurrency Stress Test (c=100, 5,000 requests)
docs.text:
Under extreme concurrency (100 concurrent workers), PyDataUI demonstrates resilience and stability, while FastAPI/Uvicorn suffers severe queuing contention on asynchronous POST:

Benchmark Workload PyDataUI (pyrustapi) FastAPI (uvicorn + uvloop) Speedup Advantage PyDataUI Latency (Mean) FastAPI Latency (Mean) Real POST (Async Pydantic) 1,172.9 req/s 220.3 req/s ⚡ 5.32x Faster 85.26 ms 453.85 ms (p99: 17.6s) Real GET (Sync) 4,066.8 req/s 1,679.0 req/s ⚡ 2.42x Faster 24.59 ms 59.56 ms Real POST (Sync Pydantic) 1,845.0 req/s 935.3 req/s ⚡ 1.97x Faster 54.20 ms 106.92 ms Real GET (Async I/O) 2,444.8 req/s 1,557.6 req/s ⚡ 1.57x Faster 40.90 ms 64.20 ms

docs.title: Profile B: Standard Load (c=50, 2,000 requests)
docs.text:
Benchmark Workload PyDataUI (pyrustapi) FastAPI (uvicorn + uvloop) Speedup Advantage PyDataUI Latency (Mean) FastAPI Latency (Mean) Real GET (Sync) 4,028.9 req/s 1,705.1 req/s ⚡ 2.36x Faster 12.41 ms 29.32 ms Real POST (Sync Pydantic) 3,736.5 req/s 1,302.3 req/s ⚡ 2.87x Faster 13.38 ms 38.39 ms Real POST (Async Pydantic) 2,311.5 req/s 1,388.6 req/s ⚡ 1.66x Faster 21.63 ms 36.01 ms Real GET (Async I/O) 2,772.4 req/s 1,966.6 req/s ⚡ 1.41x Faster 18.04 ms 25.42 ms

Key Takeaway: Under high concurrency, PyDataUI is up to 5.3x faster than FastAPI. FastAPI's event-loop queue suffers tail latency blowouts up to 17.6 seconds on async POST, while PyDataUI maintains p99 tail latency under 125 ms thanks to Tokio's multi-threaded work-stealing scheduler.

  • Identical Pydantic request models (BookInput with 5 fields including lists and floats).

docs.title: 🏗️ Why is PyDataUI Faster?
docs.text:
1. Compiled Rust Core Engine (pyrustapi):
  2. HTTP parsing, TCP socket management, keep-alive framing, and header processing are handled in compiled Rust using Tokio and Hyper.

  3. Python only executes the application logic and handler body, eliminating Python interpreter overhead for low-level HTTP protocol handling.

  4. Optimized Multi-Threaded Dispatching:

  5. Tokio distributes incoming requests across native OS threads before bridging into Python, maximizing CPU core utilization.

  6. Zero-Overhead Memory Shuttling:

  7. Request payloads and headers are mapped directly from Rust memory into Python objects via PyO3 without redundant intermediate string copying.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
Commercial-grade AI chatbot component. Features: - IME-Safe Multiline Textarea: Auto-expanding with Shift+Enter for newlines and Enter to submit. - Suggestion Chips: Clickable prompt pills (suggestions=[...]) that auto-fill and submit. - Pulsing Typing Indicators: 3-dot animation (animate-bounce) and submit button spinner during pending requests. - Auto-Scroll to Bottom: Smoothly keeps the newest messages in view on render and updates. - Markdown & Code Rendering: Assistant responses are parsed with syntax highlighting and copy button. - Dual Mode (Web & TUI): Runs in browser and in terminal with suggestion indices (1, 2) and single-key q exit.

import httpx
from pydataui import Chat, state

s = state(
    messages=[{"role": "assistant", "content": "How can I assist your team today?"}],
    session_id="chat_01",
    loading=False
)

@s.action
async def handle_message(message: str = "", **kwargs):
    user_msg = (message or kwargs.get("message", "")).strip()
    if not user_msg:
        return

    s.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_msg})
    s.loading = True

    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000", timeout=60.0) as client:
            res = await client.post("/chat/invoke", json={"id": s.session_id, "message": user_msg})
            reply = res.json().get("response", "No response")
    except Exception as e:
        reply = f"Error: {e}"
    finally:
        s.loading = False

    s.messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

@s.action
def clear_history():
    s.messages = [{"role": "assistant", "content": "History cleared. How can I help?"}]

Chat(
    messages=s.messages,
    title="Customer Support AI",
    subtitle="SLM Agent • Llama-3-8B • Context 8k",
    placeholder="Type your message... (Shift+Enter for newline)",
    on_send=handle_message,
    on_clear=clear_history,
    suggestions=[
        "How do I reset my API key?",
        "Show cluster telemetry",
        "Explain rate limit policies"
    ],
    loading=s.loading,
    height="650px",
    show_clear=True
)
Parameter Type Default Description messages List[Dict[str, Any]] [] Message list: [{"role": "user"\|"assistant", "content": "...", "timestamp": "..."}]. title str 'Agent Chat' Header title. subtitle Optional[str] None Model subtitle / cluster status in header. placeholder str 'Type your message...' Input placeholder text. on_send Callable None Async or sync function triggered when user submits a message. on_clear Callable None Function triggered when trash / clear button is clicked. suggestions List[str] [] Clickable suggestion prompt pills rendered above input. loading Union[bool, StateVar] None Triggers animated typing bubble and button spinner during API calls. height str '600px' Fixed container height with scrollable message container. show_clear bool True Displays trash icon in chat header. user_avatar Optional[str] None Image URL for user avatar. assistant_avatar Optional[str] None Image URL for AI assistant avatar. enable_markdown bool True Parses assistant messages as markdown with code syntax highlighting.

docs.title: Why PyDataUI Over Streamlit?
docs.text:
Streamlit re-executes your entire .py script from line 1 on every single user click. This creates heavy caching workarounds (@st.cache_data) and consumes high RAM per session.

PyDataUI operates on standard ASGI (Starlette / FastHTML / HTMX): 1. Event Delegation: Clicking a button or sending a message sends a lightweight HTMX POST event (/_pydataui/event). 2. Targeted Mutation: Only the targeted @s.action runs. 3. DOM Diff Swapping: Only the affected component subtree is rendered and swapped into the DOM. 4. Dual Surface: The exact same code runs in a modern web browser and as an interactive Terminal UI (TUI).

from pydataui import App, state, Button, Text, Row

app = App()
s = state(count=0)

@s.action
def increment():
    s.count += 1

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Row(
        Button("-", on_click=lambda: s.set(count=s.count - 1)),
        Text(s.count),
        Button("+", on_click=increment)
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

docs.title: Recipe 1: Zero-Class Procedural State
docs.text:
Eliminate verbose classes for rapid prototypes while retaining full reactivity.

from pydataui import App, state, Input, Button, Text, Card, Col

app = App(title="Procedural State")

# 1. Initialize state with defaults
s = state(
    query="",
    results=[],
    status="Ready"
)

# 2. Define action handlers
@s.action
def search(query: str = ""):
    val = query or s.query
    s.query = val
    s.status = "Searching..."
    # Inside actions, attributes resolve as native Python types:
    s.results = [f"Result for: {val} #{i}" for i in range(1, 4)]
    s.status = f"Found {len(s.results)} items."

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Col(
        Input(placeholder="Search docs...", on_change=search),
        Text(s.status),
        Card(
            title="Search Results",
            children=[Text(r) for r in s.results]
        )
    )

docs.title: Recipe 2: Production AI Chatbot with Loading Indicators & Modern UI/UX
docs.text:
Renders an interactive commercial-grade chat interface with: - IME-Safe Multiline Textarea: Auto-expanding with Shift+Enter for new line and Enter to submit. - Built-in HTMX Indicators: 3-dot pulsing typing bubble (animate-bounce), button spinner (animate-spin), and button/input double-submission locks (hx-disabled-elt). - Clickable Suggestion Chips: Auto-fills and triggers quick starter prompts with one click. - Auto-Scroll to Bottom: Smoothly keeps the newest messages in view on render and updates. - Markdown & Code Formatting: Beautiful syntax and styling for assistant responses with copy-to-clipboard button. - Clear Chat Support: Dedicated on_clear action handler and trash button in header.

import httpx
from pydataui import App, state, Container
from pydataui.components import Chat

app = App(title="AI Agent Chat")

s = state(
    messages=[
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "Hello! I am your AI Assistant. Ask me anything or select a suggestion below.", "timestamp": "10:00 AM"}
    ],
    session_id="chat_session_01",
    loading=False
)

@s.action
async def handle_message(message: str = "", **kwargs):
    user_msg = message or kwargs.get("message", "").strip()
    if not user_msg:
        return

    # Immediately push user message into history
    s.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_msg})
    s.loading = True

    try:
        # Non-blocking async API call to your LLM or LangGraph agent
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=120.0) as client:
            resp = await client.post(
                "http://127.0.0.1:8000/chat/invoke",
                json={"id": str(s.session_id), "message": user_msg}
            )
            resp.raise_for_status()
            reply = resp.json().get("response", "No response received.")
    except Exception as e:
        reply = f"Error: {e}"
    finally:
        s.loading = False

    s.messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

@s.action
def clear_chat():
    s.messages = [
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "Chat history cleared. How can I assist you today?"}
    ]

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Container(
        Chat(
            messages=s.messages,
            title="Customer Support AI",
            subtitle="SLM Agent • Model: Llama-3-8B • Context: 8k",
            placeholder="Type a message... (Shift+Enter for new line)",
            on_send=handle_message,
            on_clear=clear_chat,
            suggestions=[
                "How do I reset my password?",
                "What are your business hours?",
                "Show cluster compute telemetry"
            ],
            loading=s.loading,  # Triggers pulsing typing dots + button spinner
            height="650px",
            show_clear=True
        ),
        max_width="lg",
        padding="lg"
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=8000)

from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from pydataui import App, state, ShadForm, Container

class ComputeTier(str, Enum):
    STANDARD = "standard"
    ENTERPRISE = "enterprise"

class TrainingJob(BaseModel):
    experiment_name: str = Field(..., description="Unique job title")
    epochs: int = Field(10, description="Training epochs")
    learning_rate: float = Field(0.001, description="Learning rate")
    tier: ComputeTier = Field(ComputeTier.STANDARD, description="Compute tier")

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Container(
        ShadForm.from_pydantic(
            TrainingJob,
            title="Launch SLM Job",
            on_submit=launch_job

docs.title: CSS Reference for Developers
docs.text:
PyDataUI ships a small, dependency-free CSS layer for its core components and uses Tailwind CSS for utility styling and shadcn/ui tokens. This guide documents that layer for developers who are theming an application, writing custom components, or changing the framework stylesheet.

The stylesheet is a single plain-CSS file:

pydataui/styling/css/pydataui.css

There is no Sass, PostCSS, CSS-in-JS, or build step for this file. It is served unchanged at /_pdu/static/pydataui.css.

For semantic HTML APIs and generated markup, see the HTML Reference. For task-oriented examples, see UI Customization & Tailwind.

docs.title: 1. Stylesheet Architecture
docs.text:
The stylesheet is organized into numbered sections:

Section Contents 1 Reset and base element styles 2 --pdu-* design tokens and dark overrides 3 Layout: containers, flex, grid, stacks, cards, dividers 4 Typography 5 Forms and controls 6 Data display: tables, lists, badges, stats, avatars 7 Feedback: alerts, progress, spinners, skeletons, toasts 8 Navigation: navbar, sidebar, tabs, breadcrumbs, pagination 9 Overlays: modals, drawers, popovers, dropdowns 10 Media and icons 11 Animations and keyframes 12 Utility classes and responsive visibility

The layer follows three rules:

  1. Framework selectors use the pdu- prefix.
  2. Values that participate in theming come from CSS custom properties; structural values such as fixed icon sizes may remain local.
  3. Application-specific styling should use class_name or the --pdu-* tokens, not edits to framework selectors.

docs.title: Load Order
docs.text:
For a normal application page, styles are applied in this order:

Tailwind Play CDN
  -> generated shadcn CSS variables
  -> App(custom_css=...)
  -> pydataui.css
  -> App(stylesheets=[...])
  -> App(head=...)

Consequences:

  • custom_css is emitted before pydataui.css. If both rules have equal specificity, the framework rule wins.
  • External stylesheets passed to App(stylesheets=[...]) load after the framework and are the cleanest place for application overrides.
  • Inline styles passed through style={...} override both, except for !important declarations.
  • Tailwind utilities and pdu-* classes generally have equal single-class specificity. Avoid relying on source order when they conflict; use a more specific selector, an arbitrary value, or ! on the Tailwind utility.

docs.title: 2. Naming Conventions
docs.text:
Pattern Meaning Example pdu Base class added to every component <h1 class="pdu"> pdu-<block> Block or component .pdu-card, .pdu-alert pdu-<block>-<part> Part of a block .pdu-card-header, .pdu-modal-body pdu-<block>-<modifier> Variant or state .pdu-btn-primary, .pdu-tab-active pdu-<property>-<value> Utility .pdu-mt-md, .pdu-text-sm, .pdu-hidden

Names are flat, not BEM-style. Modifiers are separate classes, not descendant selectors, so an element can combine them:

<button class="pdu pdu-btn pdu-btn-primary pdu-btn-lg">Run pipeline</button>

Do not use pdu-* names for application-only classes. Prefix custom classes with your product or use Tailwind utilities. This avoids collisions during framework upgrades.

docs.text:
Use App(custom_css=...) for application-wide token changes:

from pydataui import App

app = App(
    title="Operations Portal",
    custom_css="""
    :root {
      --pdu-color-primary: #0f766e;
      --pdu-color-primary-hover: #115e59;
      --pdu-color-primary-light: #ccfbf1;
      --pdu-radius-lg: 0.75rem;

    """,
)

Token overrides inherit everywhere the token is referenced. Prefer this over copying and editing component rules.

docs.title: 4. Theme Layers and Dark Mode
docs.text:
PyDataUI has two related token layers:

Layer Variables Consumed by Framework layer --pdu-* Native pdu-* component classes and pydataui.html tags shadcn/Tailwind layer --background, --foreground, --primary, --card, --muted, --border, etc. shadcn components and Tailwind color utilities such as bg-card, text-muted-foreground

App(theme=...) controls the shadcn/Tailwind layer:

App(theme="light")  # no dark class
App(theme="dark")   # class="dark" on <html>
App(theme="auto")   # adds class="dark" when the OS prefers dark mode

App(palette=...) selects the shadcn token values. Available palettes are zinc, slate, blue, violet, green, rose, orange, and emerald.

The framework layer activates its dark token block through either .dark or [data-theme="dark"]. This means native pdu-* components follow App(theme="dark") as well:

[data-theme='dark'], .dark {
  --pdu-color-bg: #111827;
  --pdu-color-bg-secondary: #1f2937;
  --pdu-color-text: #f9fafb;
  --pdu-color-border: #374151;
  /* additional dark values */
}

To override framework dark values, put the override under the same selector:

custom_css="""
.dark {
  --pdu-color-primary: #2dd4bf;
  --pdu-color-primary-light: #134e4a;
}
"""

Because custom_css is loaded before pydataui.css, an equal-specificity .dark rule would be overwritten by the framework's dark block. Use a more specific selector or a stylesheet that loads after the framework:

html.dark {
  --pdu-color-primary: #2dd4bf;
}

docs.title: shadcn Token Names
docs.text:
The Tailwind configuration maps these utility colors to CSS variables:

Tailwind utility family CSS variables bg-background, text-foreground --background, --foreground bg-card, text-card-foreground --card, --card-foreground bg-primary, text-primary-foreground --primary, --primary-foreground bg-secondary, text-secondary-foreground --secondary, --secondary-foreground bg-muted, text-muted-foreground --muted, --muted-foreground bg-accent, text-accent-foreground --accent, --accent-foreground bg-destructive, text-destructive-foreground --destructive, --destructive-foreground border-border, border-input, ring-ring --border, --input, --ring

The shadcn values are HSL channel triplets, for example --primary: 240 5.9% 10%. They are consumed through hsl(var(--primary)), so overrides must use the same format.

docs.title: 12. Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui Integration
docs.text:
Every component accepts class_name, which is appended after its framework classes:

from pydataui.html import Section, H2, P

Section(
    H2("Pipeline health", class_name="text-2xl font-semibold tracking-tight"),
    P("Updated two minutes ago", class_name="text-sm text-muted-foreground"),
    class_name="pdu-p-lg max-w-3xl mx-auto bg-card border border-border rounded-xl",
)

Use the layers for different jobs:

Need Use Standard component appearance Native component or pdu-* class Application spacing, layout, responsive behavior Tailwind utilities in class_name Brand colors and dark-mode colors App(palette=...), tailwind_config, or shadcn token overrides Framework primitive colors --pdu-* token overrides Reusable project component Subclass Component and return pdu-* plus project classes

docs.title: Custom Tailwind Theme Values
docs.text:
App(tailwind_config={...}) deep-merges into the default Tailwind theme used by the Play CDN:

app = App(

docs.title: shadcn Component Styles
docs.text: The shadcn components are styled with Tailwind classes and the shadcn token layer, not with pdu-* classes. They follow App(theme=...) and App(palette=...) directly. To style them consistently with native components, align both token layers rather than overriding individual shadcn component classes.

docs.title: Adding a New Framework Primitive
docs.text:
1. Add a token to :root if the value should be themeable.
  2. Add a .pdu-* rule in the appropriate numbered section of pydataui.css.
  3. Reference existing tokens with var(--pdu-...) rather than repeating literal values.
  4. Add a modifier class for each variant instead of writing one-off selectors in application code.
  5. Test in light and dark mode, at mobile and desktop widths, and with keyboard focus.
  6. Update this reference if you add a public class.

Example:

.pdu-run-state {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: var(--pdu-spacing-xs);
  padding: var(--pdu-spacing-xs) var(--pdu-spacing-sm);
  border-radius: var(--pdu-radius-full);
  background-color: var(--pdu-color-bg-secondary);
  color: var(--pdu-color-text-secondary);
  font-size: var(--pdu-font-size-xs);
  font-weight: 600;
}

.pdu-run-state-success {
  background-color: var(--pdu-color-success-light);
  color: var(--pdu-color-success-hover);
}

docs.title: Adding a Custom Component
docs.text:
Prefer composing existing classes:

from pydataui import Component

class RunState(Component):
    tag = "span"

    def __init__(self, label, state="success", **kwargs):
        super().__init__(label, **kwargs)
        self.state = state

    def _get_classes(self):
        return super()._get_classes() + [
            "pdu-run-state",
            f"pdu-run-state-{self.state}",
        ]

If the component is reusable beyond one application, add the corresponding styles to the framework stylesheet and cover them with a rendering test. If it is application-specific, keep the CSS in custom_css or a stylesheet passed through App(stylesheets=[...]).

docs.title: Override Strategy
docs.text:
Choose the least invasive option that works:

Need Preferred approach One instance class_name with Tailwind utilities or an inline style One application custom_css with a scoped selector or tokens Shared across applications Framework token override or new reusable component Framework bug or missing primitive Change pydataui.css and add tests

Avoid targeting generated IDs such as #pdu-a1b2c3d4. IDs are instance-specific and are not a stable styling contract. Use classes, semantic elements, or explicit id values that you control.

docs.title: 14. Testing CSS Changes
docs.text:
CSS changes should be verified at three levels:

# Unit tests for rendering and class contracts
python -m pytest -q --ignore=tests/test_browser_security.py

# Browser tests with a real browser and stylesheet
PYDATAUI_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE="/Applications/ego lite.app/Contents/MacOS/ego lite" \
PYDATAUI_REQUIRE_BROWSER=1 \
PYDATAUI_REQUIRE_REAL_STYLES=1 \
python -m pytest tests/test_browser_security.py -q

# Documentation build
python -m mkdocs build --strict

For a manual check:

  1. Render a page in light and dark mode.
  2. Resize to mobile, tablet, and desktop widths.
  3. Confirm text and focus rings meet contrast expectations.
  4. Check that components still work when Tailwind's CDN is unavailable; core pdu-* styles should remain usable.
  5. Inspect the computed value of the relevant --pdu-* token.

docs.title: 4. Universal Extensibility Engine: Ingesting Any Upcoming shadcn/ui Component
docs.text:
"Can I use new or upcoming shadcn/ui and community components directly without waiting for PyDataUI framework updates?"

YES. Because shadcn/ui is an open registry of Tailwind CSS classes and HTML elements rather than a compiled npm package, PyDataUI lets you consume new widgets through 4 direct zero-JS pathways:

docs.title: Pathway 1: Instant JSX / HTML Copy-Paste (from_jsx & from_html)
docs.text:
Whenever you find a snippet on ui.shadcn.com, 21st.dev, or GitHub, paste the raw JSX or HTML code directly into Python:

from pydataui.shadcn import from_jsx

# 1. Paste snippet as a docstring:
UpcomingSparkCard = from_jsx("""
<div className="rounded-xl border bg-card text-card-foreground p-6 shadow-sm hover:shadow-md transition-shadow">
  <div className="flex items-center justify-between pb-2">
    <h4 className="text-sm font-medium text-muted-foreground">{title}</h4>
    <span className="text-xs font-semibold px-2 py-0.5 rounded-full bg-emerald-500/10 text-emerald-400">{status}</span>
  </div>
  <div className="text-2xl font-bold">{metric}</div>
  <p className="text-xs text-muted-foreground mt-1">{subtitle}</p>
  <div className="mt-4">{children}</div>
</div>
""")

# 2. Use immediately with typed parameters:
card = UpcomingSparkCard(
    title="Daily Active Tokens",
    status="Optimal",
    metric="4.8M",
    subtitle="Processed across 64 H100 nodes",
    children=[ShadButton("View Logs", size="sm")]
)

docs.title: Pathway 2: CLI Component Ingester (pydataui add <component>)
docs.text:
Download and generate a standalone Python component file in your project from the official shadcn JSON registry or any custom URL:

# Add official upcoming shadcn component:
pydataui add carousel
pydataui add resizable

# Add from any direct registry URL:
pydataui add https://ui.shadcn.com/r/styles/default/animated-beam.json
Use it immediately in pure Python: 
from components.shadcn.carousel import Carousel

Carousel(items=[Card(...), Card(...)])

docs.title: Pathway 3: Pure Python Declarative Factory (create_shadcn_component)
docs.text:
Define custom variants in 4 lines:

from pydataui.shadcn import create_shadcn_component

StatusBadge = create_shadcn_component(
    tag="span",
    base_classes="inline-flex items-center px-2.5 py-0.5 rounded-full text-xs font-semibold border",
    variants={
        "healthy": "bg-emerald-500/10 text-emerald-400 border-emerald-500/20",
        "critical": "bg-rose-500/10 text-rose-400 border-rose-500/20",
    },
    default_variant="healthy"
)

docs.title: 8. Advanced Animations with GSAP (GreenSock)
docs.text: PyDataUI has zero limitations on client-side animation and script libraries. You can integrate GSAP (GreenSock), ScrollTrigger, Anime.js, Lucide Icons, Canvas Confetti, and Three.js with full reactive state support.

docs.title: Loading GSAP in App
docs.text:
Pass the official GSAP CDN links directly to the scripts parameter:

from pydataui import App

app = App(
    title="GSAP Animated App",
    theme="dark",
    palette="zinc",
    scripts=[

        "https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/gsap/3.12.5/ScrollTrigger.min.js",
    ]

docs.title: Staggered Entrance & Micro-Interactions
docs.text:
Attach standard CSS classes (gsap-hero, gsap-card) to any PyDataUI or shadcn component, and embed your animation logic using Html:

from pydataui.html import Div, H1, P, Html
from pydataui.shadcn import ShadCard, ShadButton

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Div(
        H1("Fluid Animations", class_name="gsap-hero text-5xl font-extrabold tracking-tight"),
        P("60fps physics-based motion with zero configuration.", class_name="gsap-hero text-muted-foreground mt-2"),

        Div(
            ShadCard(H3("Card 1"), class_name="gsap-card p-6"),
            ShadCard(H3("Card 2"), class_name="gsap-card p-6"),
            ShadCard(H3("Card 3"), class_name="gsap-card p-6"),
            class_name="grid grid-cols-3 gap-6 mt-8"
        ),

        # Embedded GSAP Script
        Html("""
        <script>
            function runAnimations() {
                // Staggered hero text entrance
                gsap.from(".gsap-hero", {
                    y: -30,
                    opacity: 0,
                    duration: 0.9,
                    stagger: 0.15,
                    ease: "power4.out"
                });

                // Spring entrance for cards
                gsap.from(".gsap-card", {
                    scale: 0.88,
                    opacity: 0,
                    duration: 0.8,
                    delay: 0.3,
                    stagger: 0.18,
                    ease: "back.out(1.7)"
                });
            }

            // Execute on initial page load
            document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", runAnimations);

            // Re-trigger after HTMX partial page swaps (reactive updates)
            document.addEventListener("htmx:afterSwap", runAnimations);
        </script>
        """),
        class_name="min-h-screen p-12 bg-background text-foreground"
    )

docs.title: Coordinating GSAP with Reactive Server State (HTMX)
docs.text: When Python updates state on the server (e.g. via HTMX swaps), simply listen to htmx:afterSwap or htmx:afterSettle: - Initial render: DOMContentLoaded runs the entrance timeline. - Dynamic data refresh: htmx:afterSwap animates updated numbers, flash badges, or newly inserted list rows.

docs.title: 9. Working Example
docs.text:

docs.title: DataFrameTable
docs.text:
Renders a pandas DataFrame as a scrollable, styled table with shadcn design patterns.

from pydataui.components.data_science import DataFrameTable
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales_data.csv")

# Render top 50 rows
DataFrameTable(df=df, max_rows=50)

Props: - df: pandas.DataFrame instance. - max_rows: Maximum rows to render (default: 100).

docs.title: DataTable (Universal Sniffing & In-Browser Interactivity)
docs.text:
Renders any dataset with automatic schema inference, instant client-side search filtering, interactive column sorting, and pagination.

from pydataui import DataTable

# Pass Polars, Pandas, DuckDB, Arrow, Pydantic, or Dicts directly:
DataTable(
    data=df,              # Any DataFrame, Relation, Arrow Table, or list of objects
    searchable=True,      # In-browser instant text filter
    sortable=True,        # Clickable column sorting (numeric & alphabetic)
    paginated=True,       # Client-side pagination
    page_size=10
)

Supported Inputs: - Polars DataFrames & LazyFrames (df.to_dicts()) - Pandas DataFrames & Series (df.to_dict('records')) - DuckDB PyRelations (conn.sql(...)) - PyArrow Tables & RecordBatches (table.to_pylist()) - Pydantic Models & Dataclasses ([Item(...) for ...]) - Columnar Dicts ({"col": [1, 2]})

docs.title: Data Team Page Templates
docs.text:
PyDataUI ships four low-code page templates for common data-team workflows. Each template returns a normal Container component, so it works with server-rendered pages, state-driven actions, mounting, and authentication exactly like any other component tree.

Visual examples: Open the generated template gallery to see all four pages rendered in a standalone HTML page.

from pydataui import App
from pydataui.templates import analyst_dashboard

app = App(title="Analytics")

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return analyst_dashboard(
        metrics={"Revenue": "$48,250", "Orders": "1,284"},
    )

Templates are available from both pydataui.templates and the root package:

from pydataui import templates
from pydataui.templates import (
    analyst_dashboard,
    data_quality_dashboard,
    pipeline_operations,
    model_registry,
)

docs.title: Choosing a template
docs.text: Role Template Typical content Data analyst analyst_dashboard KPIs, trend chart, filters, records, CSV export Analytics engineer data_quality_dashboard Quality score, dataset catalog, schema checks, uploads Data engineer pipeline_operations Pipeline steps, inventory, activity timeline, run history ML engineer model_registry Model metrics, confusion matrix, feature importance, versions

docs.title: Shared behavior
docs.text:
• metrics accepts a mapping of label to value, or a list of dictionaries with title, value, delta, delta_type, icon, and description keys.
  • Tables accept a list of row dictionaries/lists, a component such as Table, or a pandas DataFrame (rendered through DataFrameTable).
  • Status-like columns (status, state, health, severity, stage) are rendered as colored badges.
  • Strings from application data are escaped by the underlying components.
  • Every template accepts actions=[...] for header buttons or links.
  • Aliases are available: quality_dashboard, pipeline_dashboard, and ml_registry.

docs.text:

docs.title: Analysts: pandas, Plotly, and an export
docs.text:
Templates accept a pandas DataFrame directly for the table and any component for chart slots. PlotlyChart is used here when Plotly is installed.

import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

from pydataui import App
from pydataui.components import FileDownload
from pydataui.components.data_science import PlotlyChart
from pydataui.templates import analyst_dashboard

app = App(title="Monthly Revenue")

@app.page("/")
def revenue():
    frame = pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {"month": "Jul", "region": "North", "revenue": 12400},
            {"month": "Aug", "region": "North", "revenue": 13800},
            {"month": "Sep", "region": "North", "revenue": 15100},
        ]
    )

    return analyst_dashboard(
        metrics={
            "Rows": len(frame),
            "Revenue": f"${frame['revenue'].sum():,.0f}",
        },
        chart=PlotlyChart(px.bar(frame, x="month", y="revenue")),
        table=frame,
        export=FileDownload(
            filename="revenue.csv",
            content=frame.to_csv(index=False),
            label="Download data",
            mime_type="text/csv",
        ),
    )

docs.title: Data engineers: refresh a pipeline from state
docs.text:
Templates resolve State references each render, so action handlers can update the displayed runs and metrics without bespoke frontend code.

from pydataui import App, State
from pydataui.components import Button
from pydataui.templates import pipeline_operations

class PipelineState(State):
    runs = [
        {"Run": "run_1042", "Duration": "8m 12s", "Status": "success"},
        {"Run": "run_1041", "Duration": "0m 41s", "Status": "failed"},
    ]

    def trigger(self):
        next_run = f"run_{len(self.runs) + 1041}"
        self.runs = [
            {"Run": next_run, "Duration": "running", "Status": "running"},
            *self.runs[:2],
        ]

app = App(title="Pipeline Console")

@app.page("/")
def pipelines():
    return pipeline_operations(
        metrics={"Tracked runs": len(PipelineState.runs)},
        pipeline={
            "name": "warehouse_daily",
            "status": "running",
            "steps": [
                {"name": "Extract Postgres", "status": "success"},
                {"name": "Transform with dbt", "status": "running"},
            ],
        },
        runs=PipelineState.runs,
        actions=[
            Button("Trigger run", on_click=PipelineState.trigger),
        ],
    )

docs.title: Analytics engineers: receive an uploaded file
docs.text:
DataUpload accepts either a URL or a State method. The template handles the layout; your handler validates and stores the file.

from pydataui import App, State
from pydataui.components import DataUpload
from pydataui.templates import data_quality_dashboard

class QualityState(State):
    last_file: str = ""
    last_size: int = 0

    def handle_file(self, file=None):
        self.last_file = getattr(file, "filename", "")
        self.last_size = getattr(file, "size", 0)

app = App(title="Quality Console")

@app.page("/")
def quality():
    return data_quality_dashboard(
        score=97.5,
        metrics={"Last file size": f"{int(QualityState.last_size):,} bytes"},
        datasets=[
            {"Dataset": "orders", "Owner": "finance", "Status": "Healthy"},
        ],
        issues=[],
        upload=DataUpload(
            accept=".csv,.json,.parquet",
            on_upload=QualityState.handle_file,
        ),
    )

docs.text:
Evaluation slots accept either structured dictionaries or your own PyDataUI components. This is useful when a metric needs a custom chart or annotation.

from pydataui.components.data_science import (

    FeatureImportance,
    PlotlyChart,
)
from pydataui.templates import model_registry

return model_registry(
    model={
        "name": "churn_classifier",
        "version": "v12",

    ),
    feature_importance=FeatureImportance(

        title="Drivers of churn",

docs.title: Production Deployment
docs.text: Multi-Worker & Persistent Storage: PyDataUI v0.2.1 includes a zero-infrastructure SQLite WAL storage engine (pydataui.storage). For multi-worker deployments (--workers 4+) or container volume mounts, configure PYDATAUI_STORAGE=sqlite:///var/data/pydataui_storage.db or let PyDataUI auto-configure .pydataui_storage.db. Read the production readiness guide for architecture details.

docs.title: Production Deployment Guide
docs.text: PyDataUI is designed from the ground up for high-throughput production workloads. Built on the pyrustapi engine (Rust/Tokio/Hyper), it does not require external Python application servers like Uvicorn or Gunicorn.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. One-Click Docker Build via CLI
  2. Production Dockerfile
  3. Docker Compose Deployment
  4. Kubernetes Manifests
  5. Systemd Service (Linux Server)
  6. Nginx Reverse Proxy Configuration
  7. Environment Variables Reference

docs.title: 1. One-Click Docker Build via CLI
docs.text:
PyDataUI includes an automated build command that creates a production-ready container directory:

pydataui build app.py --output dist

This packages: - dist/app.py - dist/static/ (bundled HTMX & CSS assets) - dist/Dockerfile - dist/docker-compose.yml - dist/requirements.txt

Build and run: 

cd dist
docker compose up --build -d

docs.title: 2. Production Dockerfile
docs.text:
If creating your own Dockerfile:

FROM python:3.11-slim

# Install system dependencies
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    curl \
    build-essential \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Install Python requirements
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application files
COPY . .

# Set production environment variables
ENV PYDATAUI_HOST=0.0.0.0
ENV PYDATAUI_PORT=8000
ENV PYDATAUI_DEBUG=false
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

EXPOSE 8000

# Run with pyrustapi multi-worker engine
CMD ["pydataui", "run", "app.py", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "1"]

docs.title: 3. Docker Compose Deployment
docs.text:
version: '3.8'

services:
  pydataui:
    build: .
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      - PYDATAUI_HOST=0.0.0.0
      - PYDATAUI_PORT=8000
      - PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET=${PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET:-a-very-long-production-secret-token-min-32-chars}
      - PYDATAUI_SESSION_MAX_AGE=86400
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/_pdu/health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: '2.0'
          memory: 2048M

docs.title: 4. Kubernetes Manifests
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: pydataui-app
  labels:
    app: pydataui
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pydataui
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: pydataui
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: your-registry.com/data/pydataui-app:v0.2.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        env:
        - name: PYDATAUI_HOST
          value: "0.0.0.0"
        - name: PYDATAUI_PORT
          value: "8000"
        - name: PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: pdu-secrets
              key: session-secret
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /_pdu/health
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /_pdu/health
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 2
          periodSeconds: 5
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "1000m"
            memory: "1024Mi"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: pydataui-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
  selector:
    app: pydataui

docs.title: 5. Systemd Service (Linux Server)
docs.text:
Create /etc/systemd/system/pydataui.service:

[Unit]
Description=PyDataUI Production Service
After=network.target

[Service]
User=www-data
Group=www-data
WorkingDirectory=/var/www/my-pydataui-app
Environment="PATH=/var/www/my-pydataui-app/venv/bin"
Environment="PYDATAUI_HOST=127.0.0.1"
Environment="PYDATAUI_PORT=8000"
Environment="PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET=your-32-char-random-secret-key-here"
ExecStart=/var/www/my-pydataui-app/venv/bin/pydataui run app.py --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --workers 1
Restart=always
RestartSec=3

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Enable and start: 

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now pydataui

    server_name analytics.company.internal;

    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/analytics.company.internal/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/analytics.company.internal/privkey.pem;

    # Static assets cache
    location /_pdu/static/ {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        expires 7d;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, no-transform";
    }

    # Application & HTMX traffic
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

        # WebSocket / Long-lived requests
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_read_timeout 300s;
    }
}

docs.title: 7. Environment Variables Reference
docs.text:
All PyDataUI settings can be configured via environment variables prefixed with PYDATAUI_:

Variable Default Description PYDATAUI_TITLE PyDataUI App Application browser title PYDATAUI_HOST 127.0.0.1 Network interface to bind to PYDATAUI_PORT 8000 Port number PYDATAUI_DEBUG false Enable verbose logging PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET Auto-generated Secret key for signing session cookies PYDATAUI_SESSION_MAX_AGE 86400 Session lifetime in seconds (24 hours) PYDATAUI_API_PREFIX /api Base path for auto-generated REST APIs PYDATAUI_THEME light Default theme: light or dark PYDATAUI_STORAGE Auto (memory or sqlite) Pluggable store (sqlite:///path/to/storage.db)

docs.title: 8. Production Security Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Secret Key: Set PYDATAUI_SESSION_SECRET to a high-entropy string (e.g. openssl rand -hex 32).
  • [ ] HTTPS: Terminate SSL/TLS at your load balancer or Nginx reverse proxy.
  • [ ] API Keys: Revoke test keys before promoting to production.
  • [ ] Multi-Worker Storage: Set PYDATAUI_STORAGE="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db" or let PyDataUI auto-configure .pydataui_storage.db when running multi-worker (--workers 4+).
  • [ ] CORS: Configure cors_origins in AppConfig to restrict cross-origin API calls.

docs.title: 4. Single Source of Truth Architecture
docs.text:
PyDataUI uses Markdown source files (docs/*.md) as the single source of truth. Running mkdocs build compiles all documentation pages into a complete, standalone, search-indexed HTML static site in site/:

  • 100% Offline Capable: The output directory site/ contains self-contained HTML, CSS, and JS that can be viewed locally in any browser (file:///path/to/site/index.html).
  • Full-Text Search & Dark Mode: Built directly into the compiled site without maintaining duplicate manual HTML files.
  • Automated Verification: Run mkdocs build --strict to validate all links and anchors.

docs.title: Automated CI/CD Pipeline
docs.text:
Every time a commit is pushed to the main branch affecting documentation, the GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml triggers automatically:

  1. Trigger Condition:
  2. Push to branch main
  3. Modified paths: docs/**, mkdocs.yml, .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml
  4. Or manual trigger via Actions ➡️ Deploy Documentation to GitHub Pages ➡️ Run workflow.
  5. Build Step:
  6. Installs python 3.11, mkdocs, mkdocs-material, and pymdown-extensions.
  7. Runs mkdocs build to output HTML into site/.
  8. Deploy Step:
  9. Commits and pushes the static assets to the gh-pages branch via mkdocs gh-deploy --force.
  10. Deploys live to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: 🎓 The Python Developer's Masterclass: Building Production AI APIs, Dashboards & Internal Tooling with FastAPI & PyDataUI
docs.text: A Comprehensive Guide for Python Developers, Data Scientists & AI Engineers. Learn how to turn any FastAPI AI service into a complete, enterprise-grade application with an embedded modern dashboard—in pure Python, with zero JavaScript, zero Node.js, and running on a single unified server.

docs.title: 1. Executive Vision: Why This Architecture Wins
The Core Industry Dilemma
docs.text:
In modern AI, ML, and data engineering, FastAPI is the undisputed standard. Whether you are deploying an LLM gateway, fine-tuning Mistral or LLaMA with vLLM, building RAG pipelines with LangChain or LlamaIndex, or running high-performance DuckDB and Polars queries, your backend code is almost certainly written in Python on FastAPI.

However, every production AI backend immediately needs an Internal UI: 1. Interactive Prompt & Model Playground: For engineers and domain experts to test generation parameters ($temperature$, $top_p$, stop sequences) and benchmark latency live. 2. Observability & Evaluation Dashboard: To monitor drift, hallucination rates, token throughput, and confusion matrices. 3. Internal Operations & Admin Portal: To manage API keys, inspect cluster health, approve human-in-the-loop agent steps, and review audit logs.

        F2["❌ Streamlit / Gradio\nRuns on a separate server (port 8501). Reruns the entire script on every button click, causing catastrophic 10GB model reloads and data query lag."]
        F3["❌ Reflex (Pynecone)\nTranspiles to Next.js under the hood. Requires Node.js/npm runtime, heavy WebSocket connections that lag over high latency, and confusing dual-stack stacktraces."]

        W4["✅ Universal Component Ingestion\nCopy-paste raw JSX snippets from ui.shadcn.com or 21st.dev directly into Python with from_jsx()."]
    end

docs.title: 2. The Power of High-Level Pythonic Abstractions
docs.text:
Python developers prioritize velocity, readability, and clean mental models. They do not want to spend hours debugging flexbox margins, CSS cascading conflicts, or React state hooks.

PyDataUI provides high-level, composable Python abstractions:

Abstraction What it Replaces Code Simplicity DashboardLayout 800+ lines of responsive HTML/CSS shell code Single call: DashboardLayout(sidebar=..., header=..., content=[...]) Sidebar Complex multi-tier collapsible drawer logic Pure Python dictionaries: Sidebar(brand={...}, groups=[...], footer={...}) Header Sticky navigation bar, breadcrumbs, ⌘K search trigger Single call: Header(breadcrumbs=[...], search=True, actions=[...]) ShadSlider HTML range input + value bubble + JS listener ShadSlider(label="Temperature", min_val=0, max_val=2, step=0.05, bind=State.temp) ShadRadioGroup Styled radio selection cards with descriptions Pass clean Python option dicts: [{"value": "vllm", "label": "vLLM", "badge": "Fast"}] MetricCard Custom card, status pill, badge, and delta indicator MetricCard(title="Throughput", value="1,840 tok/s", delta="+12%") ConfusionMatrix Canvas/D3 heatmaps ConfusionMatrix(matrix=[[850, 42], [38, 910]], labels=["Hallucinated", "Grounded"]) from_jsx Entire frontend component build pipeline Copy-paste JSX snippet directly into a Python string

docs.title: 3. End-to-End Master Tutorial: Building a Unified AI Service
docs.text: Here is a complete, runnable reference showing how to build an LLM Gateway with a production API and an embedded Model Evaluation Dashboard on the same server.

docs.text:
pip install fastapi uvicorn pydataui
(No Node.js, no npm, and no frontend bundler required!)

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Unified Application (main.py)
docs.text:
"""
Unified AI Inference Gateway & Operations Dashboard
FastAPI REST API + PyDataUI Dashboard running on a single Uvicorn process.
"""
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List, Optional

from pydataui import App, State, mount
from pydataui.shadcn import (
    DashboardLayout, Sidebar, NavGroup, NavItem, Header,
    ShadButton, ShadCard, ShadCardHeader, ShadCardTitle, ShadCardDescription,
    ShadCardContent, ShadBadge, ShadSlider, ShadRadioGroup, ShadDatePicker,
    ShadDropdownMenu, ShadDropdownItem, ShadDropdownSeparator, ShadTooltip,
    from_jsx
)
from pydataui.components.data_science import MetricCard, ConfusionMatrix, PipelineStatus


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Core FastAPI REST API (For programmatic clients, LangChain, SDKs)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

api = FastAPI(
    title="NeuroNest AI Inference Gateway",
    description="Production LLM endpoints with embedded internal ops portal.",
    version="1.0.0"
)

class GenerateRequest(BaseModel):
    prompt: str
    model: str = "mistral-7b"
    temperature: float = 0.7
    max_tokens: int = 512

class GenerateResponse(BaseModel):
    completion: str
    tokens_generated: int
    latency_ms: float

# Shared in-memory model telemetry state
TELEMETRY = {
    "total_requests": 14250,
    "avg_latency_ms": 14.2,
    "gpu_vram_pct": 84.6,
    "active_model": "mistral-7b-instruct-v0.3"
}

@api.post("/api/v1/generate", response_model=GenerateResponse)
async def generate(req: GenerateRequest):
    """Production endpoint used by external apps, curl, and microservices."""
    return GenerateResponse(
        completion=f"Simulated LLM completion for prompt: '{req.prompt}' using {req.model}",
        tokens_generated=len(req.prompt.split()) * 4,
        latency_ms=14.2
    )

@api.get("/api/v1/health")
async def health():
    return {"status": "healthy", "model_loaded": TELEMETRY["active_model"]}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. PyDataUI Dashboard Application (For data scientists & internal team)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

dashboard = App(title="NeuroNest Model Registry & Ops", theme="dark", palette="zinc")

class PlaygroundState(State):
    temperature: float = 0.7
    top_p: float = 0.95
    selected_engine: str = "vllm"
    benchmark_date: str = "2026-11-11"

# Extensibility Engine: Ingest an upcoming modern card without JavaScript:
BentoMetricsCard = from_jsx("""
<div className="rounded-xl border border-border bg-card text-card-foreground p-5 shadow-sm">
  <div className="flex items-center justify-between pb-2">
    <span className="text-xs font-semibold uppercase text-muted-foreground">{category}</span>
    <span className="text-xs font-semibold px-2 py-0.5 rounded-full bg-emerald-500/10 text-emerald-400">{status}</span>
  </div>
  <h4 className="text-lg font-bold tracking-tight">{title}</h4>
  <p className="text-xs text-muted-foreground mt-1">{description}</p>
  <div className="mt-4 pt-3 border-t border-border flex justify-between items-center text-xs">
    <span className="font-mono text-muted-foreground">{latency}</span>
    {action}
  </div>
</div>
""")

@dashboard.page("/")
def ops_home():
    # 1. Collapsible Sidebar Shell
    sidebar = Sidebar(
        brand={"name": "NeuroNest AI", "logo": "cpu", "plan": "Enterprise"},
        groups=[
            NavGroup("Serving & Testing", [
                NavItem("Model Registry", icon="box", href="/dashboard", active=True, badge="14"),
                NavItem("Prompt Studio", icon="sparkles", href="/dashboard/prompts"),
                NavItem("Evaluation Benchmarks", icon="activity", href="/dashboard/benchmarks"),
            ]),
            NavGroup("Operations & Telemetry", [
                NavItem("Cluster Health", icon="activity", href="/dashboard/health"),
                NavItem("Vector Stores", icon="database", href="/dashboard/vectors"),
                NavItem("Security & Audit", icon="shield-check", href="/dashboard/audit"),
            ]),
        ],
        footer={"name": "Lead ML Engineer", "email": "engineer@neuronest.ai", "avatar": "ML"},
        collapsible="icon"
    )

    # 2. Top Header with Breadcrumbs, Search, Actions, Theme Toggle
    header = Header(
        breadcrumbs=[("Gateway", "/dashboard"), ("Models", "/dashboard"), TELEMETRY["active_model"]],
        search=True,
        actions=[
            ShadTooltip("Inspect Raw Safetensors", ShadButton("Export Weights", variant="outline", size="sm")),
            ShadDropdownMenu(
                trigger=ShadButton("Deploy to Node", variant="default", size="sm"),
                content=[
                    ShadDropdownItem("Deploy to 8x H100 Cluster", icon="cpu", shortcut="⌘D"),
                    ShadDropdownItem("Deploy to AWS Inferentia2", icon="box"),
                    ShadDropdownSeparator(),
                    ShadDropdownItem("Drain Active Replicas", icon="x", danger=True)
                ]
            )
        ],
        theme_toggle=True,
        user={"avatar": "ML"}
    )

    # 3. Main Operational Content Canvas
    content = [
        # KPI Telemetry Cards Row
        MetricCard(title="Throughput", value="1,840 tok/s", delta="+12.4%", delta_type="increase", icon="📈"),
        MetricCard(title="P99 Inference Latency", value=f"{TELEMETRY['avg_latency_ms']} ms", delta="-3.1 ms", delta_type="decrease", icon="⚡"),
        MetricCard(title="GPU VRAM Allocated", value=f"{TELEMETRY['gpu_vram_pct']}%", delta="Optimal", delta_type="neutral", icon="🧠"),

        # Pipeline Execution Visualizer
        PipelineStatus(
            steps=[
                {"name": "Tokenization", "status": "completed", "duration": "1.2ms"},
                {"name": "KV Cache Lookup", "status": "completed", "duration": "0.8ms"},
                {"name": "FlashAttention-3", "status": "running", "duration": "10.4ms"},
                {"name": "Sampling & Detokenize", "status": "pending", "duration": "-"},
            ]
        ),

        # Hyperparameter Tuning Studio
        ShadCard(
            ShadCardHeader(
                ShadCardTitle("Model Generation Hyperparameters"),
                ShadCardDescription("Tune generation parameters in real-time with automatic reactive state binding.")
            ),
            ShadCardContent(
                ShadSlider(
                    label="Sampling Temperature",
                    min_val=0.0,
                    max_val=2.0,
                    step=0.05,
                    value=0.7,
                    bind=PlaygroundState.temperature
                ),
                ShadSlider(
                    label="Nucleus Sampling (top_p)",
                    min_val=0.1,
                    max_val=1.0,
                    step=0.01,
                    value=0.95,
                    bind=PlaygroundState.top_p
                ),
                ShadRadioGroup(
                    name="engine",
                    value="vllm",
                    options=[
                        {"value": "vllm", "label": "vLLM PagedAttention", "description": "High-throughput production engine", "badge": "Optimal"},
                        {"value": "tgi", "label": "HuggingFace TGI", "description": "Tensor-parallel optimized"},
                        {"value": "trt", "label": "NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM", "description": "Maximum kernel fusion speed"}
                    ],
                    bind=PlaygroundState.selected_engine
                ),
                ShadDatePicker(label="Evaluation Date Filter", value="2026-11-11", bind=PlaygroundState.benchmark_date)
            )
        ),

        # Bento Card using from_jsx extensibility
        BentoMetricsCard(
            category="Vector Database",
            status="Healthy",
            title="Qdrant Hybrid Dense-Sparse Shards",
            description="Indexing 2.4M chunks with BGE-M3 embeddings across 4 nodes.",
            latency="p99: 18.2ms",

            title="Hallucination & Factuality Evaluation"

    ]

    return DashboardLayout(
        sidebar=sidebar,
        header=header,
        content=content,
        collapsible="icon"
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The Magic Connection: Mount Dashboard into FastAPI
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# One single line connects the entire UI to FastAPI with full sub-path isolation!
mount(api, dashboard, path="/dashboard")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Entry Point Execution
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn
    # Single server command runs both the API and the full Dashboard!
    uvicorn.run("main:api", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, reload=True)

docs.title: 4. Running and Inspecting the Application
docs.text:
Start the application with a standard Uvicorn command:

Now open your browser: - Interactive Ops Dashboard: http://127.0.0.1:8000/dashboard Gives you the full collapsible sidebar, responsive header, hyperparameter sliders, confusion matrix, and ⌘K spotlight command palette. - FastAPI Interactive Swagger Docs: http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs Allows external developers to test the REST endpoints. - Automated REST Endpoint: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/generate -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"prompt": "Explain Quantum Computing"}'

docs.title: What Just Happened?
docs.text:
1. Zero Node.js was executed.

docs.title: 1. Zero-Class Procedural State Hook (state(**defaults))
docs.text:
No need to subclass State for simple tools or interactive prototypes. Declare reactive variables directly and attach functions with @s.action:

from pydataui import App, state, Button, Text, Row

app = App()
s = state(count=0, query="GPT-4")

@s.action
def increment():
    s.count += 1

@s.action
def decrement():
    s.count -= 1

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Row(
        Button("-", on_click=s.decrement),
        Text(s.count),
        Button("+", on_click=s.increment)
    )

docs.title: 2. Universal Data Sniffing for DataTable and Table
docs.text:
Pass any Python data structure directly to DataTable or Table without manual conversion:

  • Polars DataFrame / LazyFrame: DataTable(pl_df)
  • Pandas DataFrame / Series: DataTable(pd_df)
  • DuckDB PyRelation: DataTable(conn.sql("SELECT * FROM models"))
  • PyArrow Table: DataTable(arrow_table)
  • Pydantic Models: DataTable([User(id=1, name="Alice"), User(id=2, name="Bob")])
  • Dataclasses: DataTable([Metric(name="Latency", value=14.2)])
  • Columnar Dicts: DataTable({"epochs": [1, 2, 3], "loss": [0.45, 0.32, 0.21]})

Includes instant in-browser column sorting, real-time search filtering, and client-side pagination with zero JavaScript.

Avoid raw Tailwind utility classes for layout. Structure pages using clean spatial primitives:

from pydataui import Row, Col, Grid, Spacer, Card, Text

Row(
    Col(Card(Text("Model Overview")), span=4),        # 4/12 grid span
    Spacer(),                                         # Auto-flex expanding spacer
    Col(Card(Text("Live Cluster VRAM")), width="1/2") # Half width

Generate typed, validated shadcn/ui forms directly from existing FastAPI schemas:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal
from pydataui.shadcn import ShadForm

class JobRequest(BaseModel):
    experiment_name: str = Field(..., description="Unique run name")
    learning_rate: float = Field(0.001, description="AdamW learning rate")
    use_fp16: bool = Field(True, description="Enable mixed precision")
    sampling: Literal["greedy", "beam", "top_k"] = "beam"

# Instant validated form with submit button and card shell:
form = ShadForm.from_pydantic(
    JobRequest,
    on_submit=s.launch_experiment,
    submit_text="Deploy Training Run",
    field_configs={
        "learning_rate": {"component": "slider", "min": 0.0001, "max": 0.01, "step": 0.0001}

Organize multi-page applications into a pages/ directory:

PyDataUI automatically discovers the pages, registers their routes (/dashboard, /model-registry, /system-logs), parses module-level metadata (TITLE, ICON, ROLES, PUBLIC), and populates the sidebar:

from pydataui.shadcn import DashboardLayout

app = App() # auto-discovers pages/

    return DashboardLayout.from_app(app, title="Operations Center")

docs.title: FastAPI Mounting, Architecture & Conflict Handling
docs.text:
PyDataUI is designed from the ground up to be a first-class citizen in the FastAPI ecosystem. Rather than requiring a separate Node.js frontend server or fragile iframe embeds, PyDataUI applications are standard ASGI applications that can be mounted directly into existing FastAPI backends with a single line of code.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydataui import App, mount

api = FastAPI(title="Core Enterprise API")
dashboard = App(title="Executive Analytics")

mount(api, dashboard, path="/dashboard")
# or: dashboard.mount_to(api, path="/dashboard")

docs.title: 1. How FastAPI Mounting Works Under the Hood
docs.text:
When you attach a PyDataUI application to an existing FastAPI application, the following ASGI delegation flow occurs:

flowchart TD
    Client["Client Browser / Mobile Device"] -->|"HTTP Request"| ParentFastAPI["Parent FastAPI App (Uvicorn / PyRustAPI)"]

    ParentFastAPI -->|"Route: /api/v1/*"| APIRoutes["FastAPI API Endpoints & Business Logic"]
    ParentFastAPI -->|"Route: /docs"| ParentDocs["FastAPI Swagger UI (/docs)"]
    ParentFastAPI -->|"Route: /dashboard/*"| MountedSubApp["PyDataUI Sub-Application (mount)"]

    MountedSubApp --> ScopePrefix["Extract ASGI scope['root_path'] = '/dashboard'"]
    ScopePrefix --> PageRouter["PyDataUI Page Router (/dashboard/)"]
    ScopePrefix --> StateEngine["HTMX State Events (/dashboard/_pdu/event/*)"]
    ScopePrefix --> StaticAssets["Static CSS & HTMX (/dashboard/_pdu/static/*)"]
    ScopePrefix --> SubDocs["PyDataUI OpenAPI (/dashboard/docs)"]

docs.title: The ASGI Delegation Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Routing Delegation: FastAPI uses Starlette's Mount router to match any URL starting with the mounted path (e.g., /dashboard).
  2. Root Path Scoping: When the request reaches PyDataUI, FastAPI sets scope["root_path"] = "/dashboard".
  3. Context Variable Propagation: PyDataUI extracts root_path from the ASGI scope and stores it in the thread-safe _current_root_path context variable.
  4. Dynamic Path Rewriting:
  5. All internal assets (/_pdu/static/pydataui.css, /_pdu/static/htmx.min.js) automatically prefix /dashboard.
  6. All HTMX event endpoints (/_pdu/event/{state}/{method}) automatically prefix /dashboard.
  7. PWA manifest (/_pdu/manifest.json) and service worker (/_pdu/sw.js) automatically scope to /dashboard/.
  8. Authentication redirects (/login -> /dashboard/login) preserve the mount prefix.

docs.title: 2. Complete Conflict Handling Architecture
docs.text: Attaching a full-stack UI framework into an existing backend often risks route collisions, documentation overwrites, static file clashes, and cookie overrides. PyDataUI eliminates these conflicts through complete architectural sandboxing:

docs.title: Conflict Matrix & Resolution
docs.text: Potential Conflict Area Problem in Other Frameworks How PyDataUI Resolves It Gracefully Route Name Collisions Parent has /users, UI also defines /users. Strict Sub-Tree Scoping: PyDataUI routes are namespaced under /dashboard/users. Parent FastAPI's /users route remains completely unaffected. Swagger / OpenAPI Collisions Parent /docs gets overwritten or polluted with UI endpoints. Independent OpenAPI Schemas: Parent FastAPI keeps /docs. PyDataUI maintains its own isolated OpenAPI documentation at /dashboard/docs and /dashboard/api/docs. Static File Overlaps Both parent and UI use /static/*. Internal Prefix Sandboxing: PyDataUI static assets (Tailwind CSS, HTMX, Lucide) are served strictly under /_pdu/static/* (e.g. /dashboard/_pdu/static/*). Parent /static/* is untouched. Session & Cookie Overwriting UI overwrites parent auth tokens or JWT cookies. Cryptographic Cookie Scoping: PyDataUI uses a distinct signed cookie name (pdu-session) with HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax. Parent JWT, Bearer tokens, or session cookies are never modified. Middleware Interference Parent CORS, Sentry, or Rate-Limiters break UI. Layered ASGI Middleware Execution: Parent FastAPI middlewares execute before delegating to PyDataUI. PyDataUI inherits parent security policies seamlessly. Multiple UI Applications Running multiple dashboards in one API causes state cross-contamination. Instance-Level Isolation: You can mount multiple PyDataUI apps (/admin, /portal, /analytics) in the same FastAPI backend with zero state leakage.
