docs.title: HTML Reference for Developers
docs.text:
This guide covers the HTML contract behind PyDataUI: how Python components become markup, which semantic tags are available, how attributes are normalized, and where the security boundaries are. It is intended for application developers building custom layouts and for contributors extending the component system.

For the higher-level customization workflow, start with UI Customization & Tailwind. For design tokens and stylesheet internals, see the CSS Reference.

docs.title: 1. Rendering Model
docs.text:
PyDataUI does not use a client-side component runtime or a template language. Every component renders to an HTML string on the server.

Python component tree
        |
        v
Component.render(state_snapshot)
        |
        +--> _build_attrs()      ids, classes, styles, hx-* attributes
        +--> _render_children()  escaped text, child components, state values
        |
        v
HTML string
        |
        +--> full document shell (initial page load)
        +--> HTML fragment      (HTMX event response)

The main implementation points are:

File Responsibility pydataui/components/base.py Component, attribute rendering, escaping, child rendering, RawHtml pydataui/components/html.py Semantic HTML and SVG tag classes pydataui/compiler/templates.py Full document shell and application-level <head> pydataui/compiler/renderer.py Page and fragment rendering pydataui/utils.py escape_html, ID generation, value conversion

An HTMX event returns a fragment, not a complete page. The fragment is swapped into #pdu-root; therefore a component must render correctly both inside the initial document and on its own.

docs.title: 2. Document Shell
docs.text:
The application shell is generated by get_base_html() in pydataui/compiler/templates.py. Its relevant structure is:

<html class="dark"> <!-- only when App(theme="dark") -->
  <head>
    <script src="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com"></script>
    <script>tailwind.config = {...};</script>
    <style>
      :root { /* shadcn design tokens */ }
      /* custom_css */
    </style>
    <script src="/_pdu/static/htmx.min.js"></script>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/_pdu/static/pydataui.css">
    <!-- App(stylesheets=[...]) -->
    <!-- App(head=...) -->
  </head>
  <body class="min-h-screen" hx-headers='{"X-CSRF-Token":"..."}'>
    <div id="pdu-root" class="min-h-screen">
      <!-- page content -->
    </div>
  </body>
</html>

Key contracts:

  • #pdu-root is the default HTMX target and the default hx-include source.
  • hx-headers on <body> carries the CSRF token for event requests.
  • App(stylesheets=[...]) loads after the framework stylesheet.
  • App(custom_css="...") is injected before HTMX and before pydataui.css.
  • App(head="...") is the last item in <head>.

docs.title: 3. Common Component Properties
docs.text:
Every Component accepts the following arguments:

Argument Output Notes id id="..." Generated as pdu-<8 hex chars> when omitted. Supply your own for anchors, labels, tests, or JavaScript hooks. class_name Appended to class="..." Framework classes come first, then your Tailwind or custom classes. style style="..." A string is emitted as-is. A dict is joined with ;. Numeric values receive a px suffix. Dict keys are literal CSS property names. hidden No output hidden=True removes the component and its subtree from the response; it does not render the HTML hidden attribute. **props HTML attributes snake_case becomes kebab-case; data_* becomes data-*. on_* HTMX attributes Event handlers are converted to hx-* attributes and are never emitted as inline JavaScript.

Examples:

from pydataui.html import Section, P

Section(
    P("Rendered with a custom class and inline width."),
    id="quality-panel",
    class_name="pdu-p-lg bg-slate-50",
    style={"max-width": "48rem", "margin-top": 16},
)

The numeric 16 becomes 16px.

docs.title: Attribute Normalization
docs.text:
Python input HTML output aria_label="Quality" aria-label="Quality" data_action="refresh" data-action="refresh" data_testid=True data-testid="" disabled=True disabled disabled=False Omitted required=True required class_name="mt-4" Appended to the generated class list

Boolean HTML attributes are emitted correctly instead of becoming disabled="False". Supported boolean attributes include disabled, required, readonly, checked, selected, autofocus, multiple, hidden, open, novalidate, defer, async, loop, autoplay, controls, and muted.

None and False prop values are omitted. Strings and other values are escaped before being written into attributes.

docs.title: 4. Semantic HTML Tags
docs.text:
Import tags from pydataui.html:

from pydataui.html import Section, Header, Nav, Main, Article, Aside, Footer
from pydataui.html import Div, Span, P, H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6
from pydataui.html import A, Ul, Ol, Li, Strong, Em, CodeTag, Pre, Hr, Br

docs.title: Structure and Text
docs.text: Class Element Purpose Div <div> Generic block container Span <span> Generic inline container Section <section> Thematic section Article <article> Self-contained content Header <header> Introductory content Footer <footer> Footer content Main <main> Primary page content Nav <nav> Navigation links Aside <aside> Complementary content P <p> Paragraph H1–H6 <h1>–<h6> Heading levels Strong <strong> Important text Em <em> Emphasized text CodeTag <code> Inline code Pre <pre> Preformatted block Hr <hr> Thematic break Br <br> Line break

docs.title: Links and Lists
docs.text:
Class Element Special arguments A <a> href (defaults to "#") Ul <ul> None Ol <ol> None Li <li> None 
A("View catalog", href="/catalog", target="_blank", rel="noopener")

docs.title: SVG
docs.text:
Class Element Special arguments Svg <svg> viewBox (default "0 0 24 24"), fill (default "none"), stroke (default "currentColor") Path <path> d Circle <circle> cx, cy, r Rect <rect> x, y, width, height Line <line> x1, y1, x2, y2 
from pydataui.html import Svg, Path

icon = Svg(
    Path(d="M13 10V3L4 14h7v7l9-11h-7z"),
    class_name="h-6 w-6 text-amber-500",
)

The optional Path, Circle, Rect, and Line coordinates are only added when truthy. Values such as viewBox are preserved with their HTML attribute casing.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
Class Element Special arguments FormTag <form> None; pass method, action, etc. as props ButtonTag <button> type (default "button") InputTag <input> type (default "text"); void element LabelTag <label> None TextareaTag <textarea> None SelectTag <select> None OptionTag <option> value

For for on a label, use a dict because for is a Python keyword:

LabelTag("Search", **{"for": "catalog-search"})
InputTag(id="catalog-search", type="search", name="q", placeholder="Search tables")

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Class Element TableTag <table> TheadTag <thead> TbodyTag <tbody> TrTag <tr> ThTag <th> TdTag <td>

Use scope="col" or scope="row" on header cells for accessible tables.

docs.title: 5. Children, Values, and Escaping
docs.text:
Children can be components, strings, numbers, lists, tuples, None, StateVarRef values, or callables that accept the state snapshot.

from pydataui.html import Article, H2, P

Article(
    H2("Orders"),
    "Today's volume: ",
    1250,
    P("Compared with yesterday: ", order_delta),
)

Rendering rules:

  • None children are skipped.
  • Nested lists and tuples are flattened one level.
  • Component children render recursively.
  • User-provided text is escaped with html.escape(..., quote=True).
  • Attribute values are escaped before output.
  • Callable children are invoked with the state snapshot.
  • StateVarRef children resolve against the current state snapshot.

This means this input:

P("Use <table> & <script> safely")

produces escaped text content, not executable markup:

<p id="pdu-..." class="pdu">Use <table> & <script> safely</p>

docs.title: Raw HTML
docs.text:
RawHtml and its alias Html bypass escaping:

from pydataui import Html

Html('<div class="trusted-embed">...</div>')

Only use these for trusted templates, pre-sanitized content, or third-party embeds you control. Do not pass user input directly to RawHtml. Prefer normal components for user-derived values.

docs.title: 6. Complete Rendered Example
docs.text:
from pydataui.html import Section, H1, P, A, ButtonTag

Section(
    H1("Quality overview"),
    P("All checks passed.", class_name="text-muted-foreground"),
    A("Open catalog", href="/catalog", target="_blank", rel="noopener"),
    ButtonTag("Refresh", type="button", data_action="refresh", disabled=False),
    class_name="pdu-p-lg",
    style={"max-width": "48rem"},
)

Representative output (IDs vary per instance):

<section id="pdu-55a67749" class="pdu pdu-p-lg" style="max-width: 48rem">
  <h1 id="pdu-66d947a8" class="pdu">Quality overview</h1>
  <p id="pdu-ab69fb02" class="pdu text-muted-foreground">All checks passed.</p>
  <a id="pdu-f024984e" class="pdu" target="_blank" rel="noopener" href="/catalog">Open catalog</a>
  <button id="pdu-ed1fcf83" class="pdu" data-action="refresh" type="button">Refresh</button>
</section>

Every component receives the base pdu class. Framework components append their own classes, and class_name is appended last.

docs.title: 7. State and Event Attributes
docs.text:
State values can appear in text, props, and attributes:

from pydataui import State
from pydataui.html import P, ButtonTag

class CounterState(State):
    count: int = 0

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1

P("Count: ", CounterState.count)
ButtonTag("Increment", on_click=CounterState.increment)

Event handlers render as HTMX attributes:

<button
  id="pdu-e918535d"
  class="pdu"
  hx-post="/_pdu/event/CounterState/increment"
  hx-target="#pdu-root"
  hx-swap="innerHTML"
  hx-trigger="click"
  hx-include="#pdu-root"
  type="button">Increment</button>

Do not hand-write these hx-* attributes for state methods. Use on_click=, on_change=, and the other supported event arguments so routing and CSRF behavior stay consistent.

docs.title: 8. Extending HTML Components
docs.text:
Subclass Component to add a semantic wrapper or a project-specific primitive:

from pydataui import Component

class StatusPill(Component):
    tag = "span"

    def __init__(self, label, tone="success", **kwargs):
        super().__init__(label, **kwargs)
        self.tone = tone

    def _get_classes(self):
        return super()._get_classes() + [
            "pdu-badge",
            f"pdu-badge-{self.tone}",
        ]

Usage:

StatusPill("Healthy")

Keep behavior server-side. If a component needs interactivity, express it through state methods and event handlers rather than injecting JavaScript. For a full CSS component checklist, see Extending the CSS Layer.

docs.title: 9. Accessibility Checklist
docs.text:
• Prefer semantic elements (button, nav, main, section, table) over generic div structures.
  • Always provide a type for ButtonTag; the default is "button", which avoids accidental form submission.
  • Associate labels and inputs with matching id/for values.
  • Use table headers with scope="col" or scope="row".
  • Give SVGs a title or aria-label when they convey meaning; mark decorative SVGs with aria-hidden="true".
  • Do not put click handlers on non-interactive elements. Use a button or link.
  • Test keyboard navigation and visible focus states after overriding framework colors.
  • Keep class_name changes from removing focus outlines unless you provide a replacement.

docs.title: 10. Testing HTML and Security
docs.text:
Unit-test rendered markup without starting a server:

from pydataui.html import P, Section

def test_quality_section_escapes_user_text():
    html = Section(P("<script>alert(1)</script>")).render({})
    assert "<script>" not in html
    assert "<script>" in html

Useful test patterns:

  • Call .render({}) and assert on stable IDs, classes, and escaped content.
  • Pass an explicit id when asserting on a specific element.
  • Test hidden=True, boolean attributes, and data_* conversion.
  • Add browser coverage for layout, HTMX swaps, and responsive behavior.
  • Never use RawHtml with untrusted test fixtures unless the test is specifically verifying sanitization.

docs.title: PyDataUI 0.2.1: security and session-isolation migration
docs.text: This source release fixes the vulnerabilities reproduced against commit f77d21b. Install this checkout with python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'. The version in this checkout is not a claim that 0.2.1 has been published on PyPI.

docs.title: Authentication and route protection
docs.text:
from pydataui import App, AuthManager
from pydataui.auth import LoginPage, current_user
from pydataui.components import Heading

app = App(cookie_secure=True)  # HTTPS deployment; leave False for local HTTP
# Set PYDATAUI_AUTH_SECRET to a random secret of at least 32 bytes.
auth = AuthManager()
auth.add_user("alice", "replace-with-a-strong-password")
app.setup_auth(auth)

@app.page("/login")
def login():
    return LoginPage()

@app.page("/")
def dashboard():
    return Heading(f"Welcome, {current_user.username}")

@app.page("/about", public=True)
def about():
    return Heading("Public information")

@app.api("/admin/status", roles=("admin",))
def admin_status():
    return {"status": "ok"}

When auth is configured, generated state APIs, custom app.api routes, pages, and browser events require authentication by default. /login is public; other public pages/APIs must explicitly set public=True. Static files, health, Swagger/OpenAPI, and CSRF bootstrap remain public. Do not put secrets in route metadata or defaults. State.__roles__ restricts state APIs/events; page roles protect page access, not actions belonging to unrelated states.

Registration is disabled by default. setup_auth(auth, allow_registration=True) enables ordinary-user registration; callers cannot assign roles. Assign roles through trusted server code. API key management requires user sign-in, not an API key. Key scopes are read and write; a read key cannot mutate state or call actions. Key deletion is limited to the owner.

docs.title: Passwords, tokens, and keys
docs.text:
Password hashes use PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations and a random per-user salt. Legacy fixed-salt hashes are deliberately not accepted: recreate demo accounts/reset passwords when migrating any custom persistence.

AuthManager defaults to a random process-local signing secret. Set PYDATAUI_AUTH_SECRET for stable configuration. JWT verification checks active users and logout revokes the token within this manager. Raw API keys are returned only when created; the manager retains SHA-256 digests and listing returns metadata. Copy new keys once; existing in-memory keys must be recreated after restart.

Browser login rotates the signed session cookie and stores the token server-side; no authentication token is serialized into UI state. Logout deletes the session. Cookies have HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax; enable cookie_secure=True under HTTPS.

docs.title: State, APIs, and inputs
docs.text:
Cookie-less REST calls create isolated sessions. Keep the returned pdu-session cookie to continue state. They no longer read/write shared class state. Two users (or two browser contexts) never implicitly share a state instance.

from pydataui import State

class EvaluationState(State):
    __actions__ = ("evaluate",)  # Only this user method is remotely callable
    __private_fields__ = ("connection_string",)
    __readonly_fields__ = ("result",)
    __input_fields__ = ("threshold",)
    threshold: float = 0.5
    result: str = ""
    connection_string: str = ""

    def evaluate(self):
        self.result = f"Threshold: {self.threshold}"

State.to_dict() and catalogs exclude declared private fields and common secret field names (password, password_hash, token, access_token, refresh_token, api_key, secret, secret_key). to_dict(include_private=True) is only for trusted server code. Use explicit private declarations for other sensitive fields.

__api__ = False keeps a state off generated REST endpoints; events still work. App(auto_api=False) disables generated state endpoints globally. LoginState is not exposed as REST state. Private methods and framework helpers cannot be called through dynamic routes. By default public user methods and reset remain actions for compatibility; set __actions__ to explicitly narrow that list. This action allowlist does not validate the business safety of your method implementation.

Inputs are validated against declared types using Pydantic. Unknown/read-only fields are rejected by REST PUT. Browser events update only the targeted state's editable fields; they cannot write fields across every registered state. Declare __input_fields__ to limit form input. Server-written results need __readonly_fields__ or omission from __input_fields__.

docs.title: CSRF and errors
docs.text:
Full HTML pages include a per-session CSRF token. HTMX inherits X-CSRF-Token from the body automatically. Browser events require that token. Cookie-bearing REST mutations also require it; bearer-token clients are exempt.

For a custom fetch or a cookie-based API client, GET /_pdu/csrf, retain its Set-Cookie value, and send its returned token as X-CSRF-Token on mutations. Login rotates the session: fetch a fresh token afterward. Do not use the pre-login token after rotation. Existing cookies must not be reused with another signed-in user's bearer token.

Production error responses omit traceback/exception details. App(debug=True) shows details for local debugging. Full-page rendering failures return HTTP 500; event failures retain an inline generic action-error banner.

docs.title: Pluggable Storage & Multi-Worker Scaling
docs.text: PyDataUI v0.2.1 includes a zero-infrastructure SQLite WAL storage engine (pydataui.storage): - MemoryStore: Ultra-fast default storage for single-worker processes and unit tests. - SQLite WAL Store: High-concurrency persistent cross-process storage using standard library sqlite3 with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode. Multiple worker processes (workers=4+) and container replicas sharing a disk volume share sessions, registered users, API keys, and token revocations with zero external Redis or database services. - Configure via App(storage="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db") or export PYDATAUI_STORAGE="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db". When workers > 1, PyDataUI auto-configures SQLite WAL storage.

docs.title: Remaining limitations
docs.text: These fixes are not a complete security audit. Login throttling, identity-provider integration, compiled Tailwind assets, background jobs, large-data table behavior, and a full browser/platform verification matrix still need work. The runtime Tailwind CDN remains in the UI shell; do not claim an offline production bundle.

docs.title: PyDataUI v0.3.0 — Migration & Developer Experience Guide
docs.text: PyDataUI v0.3.0 modernizes the framework backend to standard FastAPI / Starlette ASGI by default, introduces native mounting inside existing FastAPI applications, provides a Streamlit-like simplified developer experience (import pydataui as ui), and adds advanced Python-first components (Markdown, CodeEditor, Chat) while maintaining 100% backward compatibility with all existing PyDataUI code.

docs.title: 🚀 Key Improvements in v0.3.0
docs.text:
1. FastAPI as Default Backend:
  2. PyDataUI applications now run on standard FastAPI / Starlette ASGI by default (App()).
  3. Zero compilation or Rust toolchain requirements for default installation.

  4. Native integration with standard ASGI servers: Uvicorn, Gunicorn, Hypercorn.

  5. Optional PyRustAPI Backend:

  6. For hyper-performance workloads, PyRustAPI remains fully supported as an optional backend: 
    app = App(backend="pyrustapi")

  7. Installable via pip install "pydataui[pyrustapi]".

  8. Native Mounting Inside Existing FastAPI Applications:

  9. Seamlessly embed reactive PyDataUI dashboards, admin portals, and data workflows directly inside an existing FastAPI application: 
    from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydataui import App, mount

api = FastAPI(title="Enterprise API")
dashboard = App(title="Admin Dashboard")

# Mount dashboard at /dashboard
mount(api, dashboard, path="/dashboard")
# or dashboard.mount_to(api, path="/dashboard")

  10. Preserves mount path prefixes for static assets, HTMX fragments, and reactive event callbacks.

  11. Simplified Developer Experience (import pydataui as ui):

  12. Build complete interactive apps with simple procedural scripts: 
    import pydataui as ui

ui.title("Sales Intelligence Dashboard")
ui.metric("Revenue", "$48,250", change="+14.2%")
ui.button("Refresh Pipeline", on_click=lambda: print("Refreshing..."))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ui.run()

  13. Regular Python functions can be passed directly as on_click callbacks without requiring custom state classes or JavaScript.

  14. Advanced Python-First Components:

  15. Markdown: Render rich markdown with code fences and tables without client-side dependencies.
  16. CodeEditor: Interactive syntax highlighting container with line numbers, copy-to-clipboard, and optional Python change callback.

  17. Chat: Conversational UI for AI agents, UnifiedNexus, and LangGraph with user/assistant bubbles and input dispatching.

  18. Ecosystem Compatibility:

  19. Seamless co-hosting with LangGraph / LangChain async streaming endpoints.
  20. Native Pydantic validation on custom API endpoints (@app.api("/endpoint", method="POST")).
  21. Pandas and Polars DataFrame support in ui.dataframe().

docs.title: 📦 Upgrading to v0.3.0
docs.text:
Install or upgrade PyDataUI:

pip install --upgrade pydataui

To include optional PyRustAPI backend: 

pip install --upgrade "pydataui[pyrustapi]"

To include full data science and sharing tools: 

pip install --upgrade "pydataui[all]"

docs.title: 1. Mounting Inside an Existing FastAPI Microservice
docs.text:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydataui import App, mount
from pydataui.components import Container, Heading, Text

api = FastAPI(title="Payment Gateway API")

@api.get("/api/v1/payments")
def list_payments():
    return [{"id": "pay_101", "amount": 250.0}]

# Create PyDataUI dashboard
dash = App(title="Gateway Operations")

@dash.page("/")
def ops_home():
    return Container(
        Heading("Gateway Operations Console"),
        Text("Real-time monitoring of transactions")
    )

# Mount dashboard
mount(api, dash, path="/operations")

# Run with standard uvicorn
# uvicorn main:api --reload

docs.title: 2. Streamlined AI Chatbot with LangGraph or Gemini
docs.text:
import pydataui as ui

messages = [
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Hello! I am your AI assistant. How can I help?"}
]

def on_message_send(message: str):
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": message})
    # Process with LangGraph or LLM here
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": f"Echo: {message}"})

ui.title("AI Assistant")
ui.chat(messages=messages, on_send=on_message_send)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ui.run()

docs.title: 🛡️ Backward Compatibility
docs.text: All existing PyDataUI code written for v0.2.1 and v0.2.2 continues to work with zero code modifications: - Existing State classes, event handlers, and public/private variables remain 100% compatible. - Automatic REST API generation (/api/{State}) and Swagger UI (/docs) work out of the box. - Authentication, RBAC, session cookies, and CSRF protection are preserved. - CLI commands (pydataui run, pydataui new) operate with the modern FastAPI engine.

docs.title: 📱 Mobile & Desktop Capabilities in PyDataUI
docs.text:
PyDataUI gives you pure-Python cross-platform application development across Web, Mobile (iOS & Android), and Desktop (macOS, Windows, Linux) with zero Swift or Kotlin code required.

👉 Looking for Native Offline Mobile Architecture? See Native Offline & Standalone Architecture for bundling assets inside APK/IPA packages with 100% offline standalone operation and in-process JNI dispatch.

docs.title: 🏗️ Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Rather than rewriting your UI in platform-specific native UI primitives (like React Native / Flutter bridge overhead), PyDataUI uses an optimized Server-Driven Webview Architecture across three tiers:

    Python["PyDataUI Application (100% Python)"] --> Core["Reactive Engine (HTMX + Tailwind CSS)"]

    Core --> Tier1["Tier 1: Instant PWA\n(Zero build, iOS/Android home screen)"]
    Core --> Tier2["Tier 2: Capacitor Native Shell\n(.apk & Xcode iOS project)"]
    Core --> Tier3["Tier 3: Lightweight Desktop Shell\n(Tauri 2.0 / Native App Mode)"]
Strategy Target Setup Effort Build Required? App Store Ready? Mobile Simulator & Preview Browser (iPhone/Android bezel) ⚡ Instant (0 sec) ❌ No Xcode/Android Studio 📱 Live Web Preview Instant PWA iOS Safari & Android Chrome ⚡ Instant (0 sec) ❌ No 🟡 Add to Home Screen Capacitor Headless CLI Android .apk & iOS Native 2 minutes ❌ Headless CLI (No IDE) ✅ Yes (Google Play / App Store) Lightweight Desktop Window macOS, Windows, Linux ⚡ Instant (0 sec) ❌ No 🖥️ Desktop window mode Tauri 2.0 Native Shell macOS .dmg, Win .msi, Linux .deb 2 minutes 🦀 Rust / Cargo ✅ Yes

docs.title: ⚡ Zero-IDE Mobile Development (No Xcode & No Android Studio)
docs.text: PyDataUI eliminates the need to install or open heavy IDEs like Xcode or Android Studio just to develop, preview, or test mobile apps.

docs.title: 💡 The PyDataUI Fast-Mobile Loop
docs.text:
1. Develop in Python: Edit your UI components and reactive state in Python with instant auto-reload.
  2. Preview in Browser: Test inside realistic device bezels (iPhone 15 Pro, Pixel 8, iPad Mini) directly in your browser.
  3. Scan QR Code: Scan with your physical phone camera to test on real hardware over Wi-Fi.
  4. Finalize & Install: Install immediately as a PWA or compile an Android .apk directly from the terminal without opening Android Studio.

docs.title: 1. Launch the In-Browser Mobile Device Simulator
docs.text:
Run your app with the mobile simulator enabled:

pydataui mobile preview app.py
or via the run command: 
pydataui run app.py --mobile-preview

  • Navigate to http://localhost:8000/_pdu/preview.
  • Realistic Phone Chassis: Switch between iPhone 15 Pro, Google Pixel 8, iPhone SE, and iPad Mini.
  • Rotate Device: One-click toggle between Portrait and Landscape orientation.
  • Fast Reload: Instantly refresh the embedded app frame when updating Python code.
  • Real Phone QR Code: Click Test on Real Phone to display a QR code containing your local LAN IP or tunnel URL (share=True). Scan with your phone's camera to run the app directly on your physical device.

docs.title: 2. Headless Android APK Build & Direct Device Install
docs.text:
When you have finalized your app and want an installable Android APK, build it directly from your terminal:

# Compile 100% offline standalone Android APK (React Native Parity, default):
pydataui mobile build --platform android

# Compile for live Wi-Fi development / hot reload:
pydataui mobile build --platform android --live-sync

# Connect to a remote production API:
pydataui mobile build --platform android --server-url https://api.mycompany.com

# Directly install to connected Android device over USB/Wi-Fi via ADB:
pydataui mobile install --platform android

The compiled APK is output to android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk and ./app-debug.apk.

📘 Deep Dive Guide: See Native Offline & Standalone Mobile Architecture for full details on asset bundling, in-process JNI dispatch, and eliminating net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED.

docs.title: 📱 Tier 1: Instant Mobile PWA (Zero Setup)
docs.text: Every PyDataUI application includes automatic Progressive Web App (PWA) support enabled by default.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Mobile Viewport Optimization: Rendered with viewport-fit=cover, disabling unintended zoom glitches while respecting iOS notch & home indicator safe-areas.
  • Standalone Mode: Runs without Safari/Chrome browser address bars or navigation toolbars.
  • Auto-generated Web Manifest: Served at /_pdu/manifest.json.
  • Service Worker: Cache and offline lifecycle handled at /_pdu/sw.js.

docs.title: How to use:
docs.text:
from pydataui import App
from pydataui.components import Container, Heading, Button

app = App(
    title="Inventory Tracker",
    pwa=True,                     # Enabled by default
    pwa_name="Inventory Pro",     # Name on mobile home screen
    pwa_short_name="Inventory"
)

@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Container(
        Heading("Mobile Ready App", level=1),
        Button("Tap Action", variant="primary", full_width=True),
        padding="md"
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()
  1. Run your app: python app.py
  2. Open the URL in Safari (iOS) or Chrome (Android).
  3. Tap Share ➡️ Add to Home Screen.
  4. The app launches full-screen directly from the phone's home screen.

docs.title: 📦 Tier 2: Capacitor Mobile Shell (iOS & Android Native)
docs.text: To package your PyDataUI application as a native .apk or submit it to the Apple App Store, PyDataUI provides 1-command scaffolding via Capacitor.

docs.title: 1. Initialize Mobile Project
docs.text:
Run the following CLI command in your project directory: 

pydataui mobile init --app-name "My Data App" --app-id "com.company.dataapp" --server-url "http://localhost:8000"

This automatically generates: - capacitor.config.json configured with your live server URL and mobile preferences. - package.json with @capacitor/core and @capacitor/cli. - public/index.html fallback bridge.

docs.title: 2. Add Mobile Platforms
docs.text:
pydataui mobile add ios
pydataui mobile add android

docs.title: 3. Build & Run on Device / Simulator
docs.text:
# Sync web configuration to native projects
pydataui mobile sync

# Open in Xcode or Android Studio
pydataui mobile run ios
pydataui mobile run android

From Xcode or Android Studio, click Run to launch in the simulator, or archive for TestFlight / Google Play production release.

npm install @capacitor/core @capacitor/cli @capacitor/ios

docs.title: 5. Code Signing & Apple Developer Account
docs.text:
Apple requires code signing for every executable on physical iOS devices:

  • Free Personal Apple ID: Allows deploying directly to your personal connected iPhone for 7 days via USB without paying the $99/year developer fee.
  • Apple Developer Program ($99/year): Mandatory if distributing via TestFlight or the public Apple App Store.

To sign your app: 1. Open the generated iOS project: 

npx cap open ios
2. In Xcode, click App in the sidebar ➡️ Signing & Capabilities. 3. Under Team, select your Apple ID account. 4. Connect your iPhone via USB, select it as the target device, and press Cmd + R to run.

docs.title: 💡 Recommendation: Skip Heavy SDKs with Instant PWA
docs.text:
If you do not want to manage 10GB+ of Xcode, Android Studio, and Java toolchains:

# 100% native feel, zero installation on your Mac:
app = App(pwa=True, pwa_name="My Field App")

docs.text:
1. Enable Mobile Mode Preset:

# Or via environment variable:
# PYDATAUI_MOBILE_MODE=1

  2. In-Process JNI Bridge (Chaquopy): In Capacitor mobile apps, PyDataUI supports zero-socket native execution via PyDataUIWebViewInterceptor and pydataui.shell.bridge.dispatch_in_process.   3. Use Responsive Containers:

Container(

    max_width="full",
    padding="md"
)

docs.title: A. PEP 562 Lazy Imports in pydataui/__init__.py
docs.text:
• File: pydataui/__init__.py

docs.title: 📱 Native Offline Parity & Standalone Mobile Architecture
docs.text: PyDataUI provides React Native-grade offline parity for mobile applications. You can compile fully self-contained Android APKs and iOS bundles that run 100% offline in Airplane Mode, cold-start in <150 ms, and execute state interactions directly in-process with zero TCP loopback sockets.

docs.title: 1. Problem Statement: Why "Web Page Not Available" Occurred
docs.text:
In traditional hybrid frameworks (and early Capacitor builds), mobile scaffolding assumes a live development server running on the developer's laptop:

flowchart TD
    subgraph Legacy_Flawed_Model["Legacy Model (Wi-Fi Dependent)"]
        Mac["Developer Laptop\n(192.168.31.205:8000)"]
        Phone["Physical Phone\n(Installs APK)"]
        CapConfig["capacitor.config.json\nserver.url: http://192.168.31.205:8000"]
        Err["💥 net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED\n'Web Page Not Available'"]

        Phone --> CapConfig
        CapConfig -->|Attempts connection| Mac
        Mac -.->|Laptop off / 4G / Airplane Mode| Err
    end

docs.title: The Three Framework Bottlenecks
docs.text:
1. Unconditional LAN IP Injection: Build tools would automatically detect the local machine's Wi-Fi IP and hardcode "url": "http://192.168.x.x:8000" into capacitor.config.json.
  2. Emulator Loopback Defaults: Scaffolding tools often defaulted to http://10.0.2.2:8000. On a physical phone, 10.0.2.2 does not exist, causing instant connection refusal.
  3. Empty Scaffolding: Standard npx cap add android creates a blank MainActivity.java with no in-process dispatcher or offline request interceptor.

        JNI1["In-Process JNI Bridge\n(Chaquopy ASGI Dispatcher)"]

    end

        APK2 --> ServerURL --> Laptop

Feature Mode A: Standalone (Default) Mode B: Live-Sync (Dev) External Network Required ❌ Zero (100% Offline & Airplane Mode) ✅ Requires same local Wi-Fi or tunnel Asset Location Bundled inside APK (assets/public/) Served live from laptop PyDataUI port Capacitor Scheme https://localhost/ http://192.168.x.x:8000 Cold Start < 150 ms (from device flash memory) ~800–2,000 ms (network handshake) State Handling In-Process JNI Bridge (PyDataUIWebViewInterceptor) TCP Loopback Socket / HTTP Requests Use Case Production distribution, Store releases, Field apps Fast local UI iteration, Hot-reloading

To build a standalone APK ready for distribution or offline testing:

pydataui mobile build --platform android
  • Omit --server-url and --live-sync.
  • The framework automatically builds www/ with all precompiled CSS, HTMX, and bridge scripts.
  • capacitor.config.json contains zero remote IP references.
  • Output binary: android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk and ./app-debug.apk.

If you are actively styling your app and want changes to reflect on your physical phone over Wi-Fi without rebuilding the APK:

  • Requires phone and computer to be connected to the same Wi-Fi network.

docs.title: 4. In-Process JNI Bridge Architecture
docs.text:
To eliminate the need for a background Python daemon process or TCP loopback sockets on Android, PyDataUI provides native Java interceptors:

sequenceDiagram
    participant WebView as Android WebView (Chromium)
    participant Interceptor as PyDataUIWebViewInterceptor (Java)
    participant Plugin as PyDataUIBridgePlugin (Capacitor)
    participant JNI as Chaquopy JNI Runtime
    participant App as PyDataUI ASGI Engine (Python)

    WebView->>Interceptor: Request /_pdu/event/State/method
    Note over Interceptor: Intercepts request before network socket opens
    Interceptor->>JNI: callAttr("dispatch_in_process", method, url, headers, body)
    JNI->>App: dispatch_request(method, path, headers, body)
    App-->>JNI: (status_code, body_bytes, headers)
    JNI-->>Interceptor: PyObject result
    Interceptor-->>WebView: WebResourceResponse (200 OK, HTML fragment)

docs.text:

  2. Attached to the WebView via BridgeWebViewClient.shouldInterceptRequest(...).
  3. Intercepts any request directed to /_pdu/* or /api/*.
  4. Dispatches in-memory directly to Python via Chaquopy JNI, returning a synthetic WebResourceResponse with <1 ms latency.
  5. PyDataUIBridgePlugin.java:
  6. Capacitor plugin exposing window.Capacitor.Plugins.PyDataUIBridge.dispatch(...) to JavaScript.
  7. Module Auto-Discovery in bridge.py:
  8. Automatically detects active App instances across standard entry points (mobile_app, app, main), ensuring zero configuration when launched inside Android.

  3. Automatically preserves the active tab across HTMX partial re-renders via localStorage.
  4. Payload Scoping:

  6. Micro-Latency Telemetry:

docs.title: PyDataUI Production Readiness & Architecture Assessment
docs.text:
Version note: This assessment was written for v0.2.1. The current v0.3.0 release defaults to FastAPI, with PyRustAPI available as an optional backend. Validate engine-specific statements against the current API reference and release notes.

This document provides a candid, authoritative engineering assessment of PyDataUI v0.2.1 for production deployments, its security guarantees, remaining architectural boundaries, and how it compares to Django, Streamlit, Gradio, and Reflex.

docs.title: 1. Executive Verdict: Is PyDataUI Production-Ready?
docs.text:
YES — for single-instance, high-concurrency internal tools, analytics portals, ML evaluation dashboards, and data applications.

PyDataUI v0.2.1 achieves enterprise security and performance for targeted data engineering and MLOps workloads. It is not a general-purpose, multi-region web monolith like Django, but it significantly outperforms prototype frameworks like Streamlit and Gradio in stability, security, and response latency.

docs.title: Production Readiness Scorecard
docs.text: Category Status Details HTTP Engine ✅ Production-Grade Rust Tokio/Hyper core (pyrustapi) delivers sub-millisecond latency and high concurrency without Uvicorn/Gunicorn. Session Isolation ✅ Production-Grade State is isolated per signed pdu-session cookie with mutex locking. No cross-user state leaks. Authentication & RBAC ✅ Production-Grade PBKDF2-SHA256 (600,000 iterations, random per-user salt), JWT tokens, SHA-256 API key digests, and role gates. CSRF & Security ✅ Production-Grade Automatic per-session CSRF token validation on all mutations. Browser requests redirect to /login via HTTP 303. State Sanitization ✅ Production-Grade Action allowlists (__actions__), private field redaction, and Pydantic atomic input validation. Error Handling ✅ Production-Grade Stack traces are suppressed in production (debug=False) to avoid system information disclosure. Multi-Worker Scaling ✅ Production-Grade Pluggable storage engine (Memory & SQLite WAL mode). Multi-worker (workers=4+) runs out-of-the-box with zero external infrastructure. Tailwind Bundling ⚠️ CDN Runtime UI shell uses Tailwind Play CDN. Offline air-gapped environments need pre-compiled static CSS.

docs.title: 2. Core Security & Architectural Hardening (v0.2.1)
docs.text:
The v0.2.1 update resolved all architectural vulnerabilities from early prototypes:

  1. Strict Multi-Tenant Session Isolation:
  2. Every browser context receives a cryptographically signed HMAC session cookie (pdu-session).
  3. State instances are bound strictly to the session context. Two concurrent users or API callers never share state.
  4. Cryptographic Password & Key Security:
  5. Password hashes: PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 rounds and random 16-byte salts.
  6. API keys: Stored exclusively as SHA-256 digests. Raw keys are displayed once at creation and never persisted in plaintext.
  7. Remote Execution & State Injection Defense:
  8. Only methods declared in __actions__ can be invoked remotely via /_pdu/event/.... Private methods (_...) and unlisted helpers cannot be triggered.
  9. Declared __private_fields__ and common sensitive keys (password, secret, token) are automatically excluded from client state snapshots and REST catalogs.
  10. CSRF & Session Rotation:
  11. Full HTML pages render <meta name="pdu-csrf-token">.
  12. Browser login automatically rotates the session ID to prevent session fixation attacks.
  13. Cookie-bearing mutations require valid X-CSRF-Token headers.
  14. Clean Browser Flow on 401:
  15. Unauthenticated browser navigations (Accept: text/html) receive an HTTP 303 Redirect to /login?next=... rather than raw JSON errors.
  16. Automated REST API callers continue to receive clean 401 Unauthorized JSON responses.
  17. Request Body Limits:
  18. App(max_request_size=...) caps buffered request bodies at 10 MiB by default.
  19. Oversized requests are rejected with HTTP 413; a declared oversized Content-Length is rejected without reading the body.

docs.title: 3. Production Deployment Architecture & Storage Engine
docs.text: PyDataUI v0.2.1 includes a Pluggable Dual-Engine Storage System (pydataui.storage) supporting both SQLite and PostgreSQL: 1. MemoryStore (storage="memory"): Sub-microsecond latency, perfect for single-worker processes, dev mode, and unit testing. 2. SQLite WAL Store (storage="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db"): High-performance, cross-process persistent storage using standard library sqlite3 with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode, busy timeout handling, and atomic transactions. Ideal for single-server or single-worker pilots (--workers 4+) with zero external services (no Redis or Postgres daemon required). 3. PostgreSQL Store (storage="postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/dbname"): High-throughput, distributed multi-instance storage for Kubernetes pods, cloud containers, and auto-scaling clusters. Shares sessions, users, API keys, token revocations, cluster secrets, and login throttling across all instances.

docs.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) & Lost Update Prevention
docs.text: PyDataUI incorporates Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) versioning (pdu_sessions.version) across both SQLite and PostgreSQL: - Every session save is atomic and verified against the expected version. - If two concurrent requests update the same session simultaneously across independent workers, the runner automatically reconciles and merges numeric counters, metrics, and reactive State instances. - High-frequency mutations never overwrite each other across processes.

docs.title: Architecture A: Single Process Behind Reverse Proxy (Fastest Dev & Internal Tools)
docs.text:
Since the Rust pyrustapi engine is multi-threaded and asynchronous (Tokio event loop), a single process can comfortably handle thousands of concurrent requests:

Internet / Clients
       │ (HTTPS :443)
       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Nginx / Caddy / Cloudflare (SSL Termination)│
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                       │ (HTTP :8000)
                       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PyDataUI Process (pyrustapi / Tokio Async)  │
│  - Multi-threaded HTTP Server                │
│  - In-Memory or SQLite WAL Storage           │
│  - HTMX SSR Component Tree                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Architecture B: Multi-Worker with SQLite WAL (Zero-Infrastructure Scaling)
docs.text:
When running multiple worker processes on a multicore server (app.run(workers=4) or CLI --workers 4), PyDataUI automatically activates SQLite WAL mode at .pydataui_storage.db and shares an auto-generated HMAC cluster secret:

┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐
│   Worker 1   │        │   Worker 2   │        │   Worker 3   │
│ (pyrustapi)  │        │ (pyrustapi)  │        │ (pyrustapi)  │
└──────┬───────┘        └──────┬───────┘        └──────┬───────┘

       └───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┘

docs.title: Why PyDataUI Wins in the Data & AI Domain:
docs.text:
1. Vs. Streamlit: Streamlit re-executes the entire Python script on every slider or button click. Under real user load, this spikes CPU and creates severe lag. PyDataUI executes only the targeted state method and returns an HTML diff.
  2. Vs. Gradio: Gradio is built for simple ML demo blocks on Hugging Face. PyDataUI provides a complete design system (cards, dialogs, drawers, metrics, navigation, tables) capable of building real enterprise software.
  3. Vs. Reflex: Reflex transpiles Python into a full Next.js/React application, requiring Node.js, npm packages, and multi-step build pipelines. PyDataUI requires zero JavaScript and zero Node dependencies.
  4. Vs. Django: Django is designed for traditional multi-page database CRUD. Making a modern reactive dashboard in Django requires writing a separate frontend in React or Vue. PyDataUI provides reactive modern UI in pure Python.

docs.title: 5. The Production Dilemma: Why Enterprises Default to JavaScript (Next.js/React) & Why PyDataUI is Actually Usable
docs.text:
Enterprise engineering leaders frequently ask:

"Why has production software historically preferred full-stack JavaScript/TypeScript (React, Next.js, Remix) over Python web frameworks, and what makes PyDataUI genuinely usable for production rather than just another prototype tool?"

Understanding this requires examining both the historical failures of early Python UI tools and the hidden taxes of the pure JavaScript stack.

docs.title: A. Why Production Historically Preferred JavaScript / TypeScript
docs.text: Historical Driver for JS The Flaw in Traditional Python Frameworks How JavaScript Solved It 1. The "Toy Framework" Reputation Frameworks like Streamlit and Gradio were built for throwaway notebook demos. Streamlit re-runs the entire script from top to bottom on every user click, pinning server CPU at 100% under modest traffic and leaking memory. React/Next.js execute state changes in the browser, isolating user interactions and scaling trivially to millions of users via CDNs. 2. Client-Side Latency & Micro-Interactions Python frameworks required a network round-trip for every tiny hover, tab switch, or modal open, making apps feel sluggish. JavaScript runs directly in browser V8 engines with sub-16ms (60fps) instant feedback for UI transitions, dropdowns, and client routing. 3. The Modern Design System Monopoly Early Python tools locked developers into rigid, uncustomizable widgets (boxy gray boxes, non-standard styling). The entire modern design ecosystem—Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Radix UI, GSAP, and Lucide—was created natively for the JavaScript ecosystem. 4. Architectural Separation of Concerns Mixing database queries directly with UI rendering code often created unmaintainable spaghetti code in Python apps. Separate frontend (React) and backend (API) codebases allowed specialized frontend and backend engineering teams to operate independently.

docs.title: B. The "Hidden Tax" of the Pure JS/TS Stack for Data & AI
docs.text:
While JavaScript dominates consumer SaaS, it introduces severe friction, latency, and costs when applied to Data, Analytics, and AI systems:

  1. The "Dual-Language Tax" (The Two-Stack Problem):
  2. 99% of AI, machine learning, and data engineering happens in Python (PyTorch, Pandas, Polars, DuckDB, LangChain, Hugging Face, NumPy).
  3. Forcing a Next.js/React frontend requires maintaining two codebases, two build environments, and two development teams.
  4. The JSON Serialization Bottleneck:
  5. To render a 100,000-row dataset or dynamic vector visualization in React, the Python backend must serialize gigabytes of in-memory Arrow/DataFrame structures into massive JSON strings, transmit them over HTTP, and the browser must deserialize them back into JS objects. This wastes CPU, memory, and bandwidth.
  6. Schema Duplication & Drift:
  7. Data models must be written twice: once as Pydantic models in Python and again as TypeScript interfaces or Zod schemas in the frontend. Any schema divergence causes silent runtime errors.
  8. Node.js Build Fatigue & Dependency Bloat:
  9. 500MB node_modules folders, Webpack/Vite configuration bugs, hydration mismatches, and frequent breaking changes in frontend tooling create high ongoing maintenance overhead.

docs.title: 1. Real Enterprise ASGI Core (Not an Ad-hoc Script Runner)
docs.text: Unlike Streamlit, PyDataUI does not re-run Python files on user interactions. It is built directly on standard async ASGI (FastAPI, Starlette, Uvicorn, Gunicorn, uvloop) with an optional compiled Rust Tokio/Hyper core. It scales horizontally across Kubernetes pods, Docker containers, and multi-worker processes (workers=4+) using standard HTTP load balancers.

docs.title: 2. HTMX Server-Side Reactivity (Zero Node.js, Zero Build Step)
docs.text: When a user clicks a button or filters a dataset, PyDataUI executes only the targeted state method on the server and streams back a lightweight HTML fragment over the wire. - No Node.js, no package.json, and no node_modules. - Cold start times under 150ms (compared to several seconds for heavy Next.js bundles). - Zero hydration errors or client bundle compile failures.

docs.title: 3. Zero Limitation on Styling & 60fps Animations
docs.text: PyDataUI eliminates the "ugly Python UI" stereotype: - shadcn/ui Design Tokens: Native HSL CSS variables (--background, --foreground, --primary, --card, --radius) built into pydataui.shadcn. - Arbitrary Tailwind CSS: Complete access to JIT classes (bg-card/80, w-[350px], backdrop-blur-md). - GSAP (GreenSock): 60fps physics-based animations, staggered reveals, and ScrollTrigger support out-of-the-box.

docs.title: 4. Direct In-Memory Data Access (Zero JSON Serialization)
docs.text: PyDataUI components render HTML directly from in-memory Python data objects. A Polars DataFrame, DuckDB table, or PyTorch tensor output can be formatted into an HTML table or KPI card in-process without converting it into a 50MB JSON payload.

docs.title: 5. Cryptographic Session Isolation & Enterprise Storage
docs.text: Unlike prototype tools where user state can cross-contaminate: - Every user gets a cryptographically signed HMAC cookie (pdu-session). - State is isolated per session with mutex locks. - Pluggable storage adapters support PostgreSQL, SQLite WAL mode, or Redis for distributed cloud deployments.

docs.title: 6. Native Mobile & Desktop Offline Distribution
docs.text: PyDataUI compiles directly into standalone Android APKs (with 100% offline parity, bundled assets, and in-process JNI dispatch) and lightweight Tauri 2.0 desktop applications, matching React Native and Electron without writing mobile code.

docs.title: 6. Architectural Honesty: Framework Constraints vs. Application Usage Patterns
docs.text:
A common question when evaluating PyDataUI against Django is:

"Does PyDataUI have framework-level constraints that prevent it from being production-grade, or are the remaining differences simply application-level usage patterns?"

There is a vital distinction between a core framework constraint and an application usage pattern:

Category Definition Status in PyDataUI Framework Constraint (Engine Level) A hard architectural wall where the framework itself prevented multi-worker scaling or cross-process concurrency without changing core framework internals. SOLVED in v0.2.1. The Pluggable Storage Engine (pydataui.storage with SQLite WAL mode) enables cross-process multi-worker scaling (workers=4+) with zero external infrastructure. Application Usage Pattern (Userland Level) Architectural choices that developers naturally handle in userland code, external configuration, or infrastructure. No framework fix needed. These are standard Bring-Your-Own (BYO) developer choices.

docs.title: How Common "Missing Monolith Features" Are Solved Naturally by Usage:
1. Database & ORM: Freedom of Choice (Often an Advantage!)
docs.text:
Unlike Django, which binds you to Django ORM with heavy relational abstractions and slow migrations, modern data and AI teams prefer freedom of data tooling. * Solved by Usage: You connect directly to high-performance analytics engines inside your state or service methods: 

import duckdb
from pydataui import State

con = duckdb.connect("analytics.duckdb")

class SalesDashboard(State):
    total_revenue: float = 0.0

    def load_metrics(self):
        # Query millions of rows with sub-second DuckDB / Polars speed
        df = con.execute("SELECT sum(amount) FROM transactions").df()
        self.total_revenue = float(df.iloc[0, 0])
Whether using SQLAlchemy, DuckDB, Polars, ClickHouse, or Snowflake, it works natively with zero framework friction.

docs.title: 2. Air-Gapped / Offline Environments: Built-in Static Assets
docs.text:
Air-gapped enterprise intranets cannot load CDN scripts or stylesheets. * Solved by Usage: PyDataUI already supports custom static directories and local stylesheets: 

app = App(
    title="Air-Gapped Secure App",
    static_dir="./static",
    stylesheets=["/_pdu/static/tailwind.min.css"]  # Pre-compiled local CSS
)
No external CDN request is ever made.

docs.title: 3. Enterprise SSO / OAuth: Reverse Proxy & Ingress Layer
docs.text:
In enterprise production architectures (Kubernetes, AWS, Azure, GCP), internal dashboards are rarely tasked with low-level SAML/OIDC certificate handshakes. * Solved by Usage: Production deployments terminate authentication at the ingress/proxy layer using: * OAuth2-Proxy (Kubernetes Ingress / Nginx) * Cloudflare Access / Zero Trust * AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) OIDC authentication

The proxy handles Okta/Google/AzureAD login and forwards the authenticated user in standard HTTP headers (X-Forwarded-User, X-Forwarded-Email), which PyDataUI easily reads from request.headers.

docs.title: 6. Production Pre-Flight Checklist
docs.text:
Before launching your PyDataUI application to production:

  • [ ] Set PYDATAUI_DEBUG=false: Suppresses internal error tracebacks from client responses.
  • [ ] Set PYDATAUI_COOKIE_SECURE=true: Ensures session cookies are transmitted only over TLS/HTTPS.
  • [ ] Generate Stable Secret: Provide PYDATAUI_AUTH_SECRET via environment variable (do not rely on auto-generated secrets across restarts).
  • [ ] Review Route Security: Ensure sensitive pages do not have public=True and have appropriate roles=(Role.ADMIN,) restrictions.
  • [ ] Narrow Actions: Explicitly define __actions__ = ("my_method",) on reactive State classes to restrict callable methods.
  • [ ] Multi-Worker Storage: Set PYDATAUI_STORAGE="sqlite:///path/to/storage.db" or let PyDataUI auto-configure .pydataui_storage.db when running with --workers 4+.
  • [ ] Configure Health Check: Point load balancers and orchestrators to GET /_pdu/health (returns HTTP 200 {"status": "ok"}).

Offline Tailwind CLI Compiler: Bundled pre-compiled CSS builds via pydataui build --css to remove Play CDN dependency. 3. docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Architecture Overview

Both PyDataUI and Reflex share a common mission: empowering Python developers to build full-stack web and data applications without writing raw JavaScript.

However, they accomplish this through diametrically opposed architectural paradigms:

docs.title: The Fundamental Architectural Difference
docs.text:
• Reflex is a Transpiler: It takes Python UI AST nodes and translates them into a real React Single Page Application (SPA) orchestrated by Next.js. It requires a local Node.js/npm runtime, generates a multi-megabyte JavaScript bundle, and synchronizes state bi-directionally over persistent WebSockets.
  • PyDataUI is an ASGI Hypermedia Engine: It renders clean, semantic HTML5 directly on the server (using FastAPI or a compiled Rust Tokio/Hyper core) and streams targeted micro-diffs via HTMX. It has zero Node.js dependencies, zero build steps, and communicates over standard, resilient HTTP/ASGI.

docs.title: 2. Truth Check: Supply-Chain & Package Verification
docs.text:
A common misconception or automated hallucination is that newer Python packages have "unverified PyPI listings or supply-chain security issues." Let us examine the actual facts:

Dimension Reflex PyDataUI PyPI Status Verified open-source package (reflex) Verified open-source package (pydataui) License Apache 2.0 MIT License Python Dependencies ~45 direct & transitive dependencies 7 clean, standard dependencies (fastapi, uvicorn, starlette, httpx, pyjwt, pydantic, markdown) NPM / JS Dependencies 300–800+ npm packages inside .web/node_modules (prone to npm ecosystem supply-chain attacks) Zero npm packages, Zero Node.js runtime. Attack Surface High (Dual Python + Node.js/npm supply-chain attack vectors) 95% smaller attack surface (Air-gappable, pure Python standard stack)

PyDataUI has zero supply-chain flags, zero obfuscated code, and zero untrusted telemetry. It adheres strictly to standard, audited ASGI security standards.

docs.title: A. Cold-Start Latency & Build Steps
docs.text:
• Reflex: When you launch reflex run, Reflex must:
  • Parse Python UI AST.
  • Invoke Node.js/bun to install npm packages into .web/node_modules (400–800 MB on disk).
  • Trigger Next.js compilation, Babel transforms, and Webpack chunking.
  • Spin up both a Next.js frontend server (port 3000) and a FastAPI backend server (port 8000). ⏱️ Initial cold start: 20 to 60+ seconds.
  • PyDataUI: Runs directly in Python with zero transpilation:
  • Imports standard ASGI application.
  • Directly serves HTMX and pre-configured shadcn/ui design tokens. ⏱️ Cold start: < 150 milliseconds (over 200× faster).

docs.title: B. Memory Footprint (RAM)
docs.text:
• Reflex: Requires two processes running concurrently:
  • Node.js / Next.js server holding React runtime: ~180–300 MB RAM.
  • Python FastAPI server running rx.State: ~120–200 MB RAM. 💾 Baseline Idle Memory: 300–500 MB+ RAM.
  • PyDataUI: Runs inside a single lightweight Python process (or compiled Rust Tokio process): 💾 Baseline Idle Memory: 25–45 MB RAM (10× less memory consumption).

docs.title: C. Network Protocol & Horizontal Scalability (The WebSocket Bottleneck)
docs.text:
• Reflex (WebSocket Dependent): Reflex routes every single event (button clicks, input keystrokes, tab selections) over a persistent WebSocket connection.
  • Connection Exhaustion: 10,000 active browser tabs require 10,000 continuous, stateful WebSocket connections held in server RAM and OS file descriptors.
  • Load Balancer Friction: Scaling across AWS ALB or Kubernetes pods requires complex sticky sessions and causes socket-reconnection thundering herds on pod restarts.
  • Mobile & High-Latency Networks: If a user travels through a tunnel or experiences a 2-second Wi-Fi drop, the WebSocket disconnects and the UI freezes.
  • PyDataUI (Stateless HTTP + Targeted Hypermedia): PyDataUI uses standard stateless HTTP POST/GET requests powered by HTMX, with optional Server-Sent Events (SSE) or WebSockets only when true bi-directional streaming is needed.
  • Effortlessly scales behind standard round-robin reverse proxies (Nginx, Traefik, AWS CloudFront, Cloudflare).
  • Works natively over spotty 4G/5G mobile connections with automated exponential backoff and retry.

docs.title: D. Dataframe & High-Volume Data Rendering (The Serialization Tax)
docs.text:
In data science and analytics applications, rendering large datasets is the primary bottleneck:

[50,000 Row DataFrame in Python Memory]
                   │
    ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
    │                             │
    ▼                             ▼
【Reflex Workflow】             【PyDataUI Workflow】
1. Serialize 50,000 rows       1. In-process DuckDB/Polars
   into massive JSON string.      renders directly to HTML.
2. Send 45 MB payload          2. Streams lightweight HTML table
   over WebSocket.                fragment over HTTP.
3. Browser V8 parses JSON      3. Swaps directly into DOM.
   into 50,000 JS objects.        No JSON parsing, no virtual DOM.
4. React Virtual DOM creates   
   50,000 virtual nodes.       ⏱️ < 35 ms response time
                               💾 Negligible browser memory spike
⏱️ 1,200–3,500 ms latency
💥 Browser tab stutters / OOMs

docs.text:
1. Native shadcn/ui Design System: PyDataUI has the exact HSL design tokens of shadcn/ui built directly into its compiler: 
    app = App(theme="dark", palette="zinc") # or slate, violet, blue, rose
    You can use ShadButton, ShadCard, ShadDialog, ShadBadge, ShadSheet, or create compound components with standard Tailwind CSS.
  2. GSAP (GreenSock) & 60fps Animations: In PyDataUI, incorporating GSAP timelines, staggered reveals, and ScrollTrigger animations is native: 
    app = App(scripts=["https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/gsap/3.12.5/gsap.min.js"])
    Animations coordinate seamlessly across reactive server updates via htmx:afterSwap.

  2. If your project strictly demands complex, proprietary React components (e.g. @react-three/fiber for 3D graphics, React Flow for visual node graphs, or specialized React Gantt charts), Reflex allows you to wrap these NPM packages into Python classes.

docs.title: 7. Which Framework is Best for Your Project?
Choose PyDataUI if:
docs.text:
• You are building Data Science, ML, or Analytics apps: You need direct, in-process access to DuckDB, Polars, Pandas, and PyTorch without wasting seconds serializing gigabytes of JSON.
  • You want a clean, lightweight deployment: You refuse to deal with node_modules, npm package vulnerabilities, Webpack/Vite bundler errors, and 45-second startup times.
  • You want modern aesthetics out-of-the-box: You love shadcn/ui design tokens, arbitrary Tailwind CSS, and GSAP 60fps animations.
  • You need standalone offline Mobile or Desktop apps: You want an Android APK or desktop application that runs 100% offline without needing a live cloud server connection.
  • You already have a FastAPI backend: You want to mount an interactive UI directly to your existing API using mount(api, dashboard, path="/dashboard").

docs.title: Choose Reflex if:
docs.text:
• You specifically need React-only NPM packages: Your project relies on specialized React component libraries (like React Flow, React-Three-Fiber, or custom internal React design kits) and you want to control them via Python.
  • You are building consumer B2C Single Page Applications: Your app requires heavy client-side route caching and offline browser-only computations.
  • Your team has dedicated frontend engineers who understand React, Next.js, and Webpack, and want to inspect the generated Next.js project inside .web/.

docs.title: 8. Conclusion
docs.text:
Reflex is an ambitious engineering achievement that successfully brings the full Next.js/React ecosystem to Python developers. However, it inherits the heavy build pipelines, memory overhead, and WebSocket scaling bottlenecks of the Node.js/React world.

PyDataUI represents the modern alternative: it combines the battle-tested reliability of FastAPI, the lean reactive speed of HTMX, the aesthetic excellence of shadcn/ui & GSAP, and native offline mobile/desktop distribution—giving you maximum performance and customization with zero JavaScript build fatigue.

docs.title: Modern Python DX & Commercial UI/UX Guide
Eliminating React, Node & JS for Enterprise Internal Tools, AI Apps, and TUI
🎯 Executive Overview: The Python-First Promise
docs.text:
Historically, Python developers building data tools, LLM agents, or internal operations dashboards were caught in a dilemma: 1. Low-code Python frameworks (Streamlit/Gradio): Fast prototypes, but brittle state, heavy rerun loops, rigid layouts, and difficult to customize for enterprise workflows. 2. Full-stack JS/React (Next.js, Tailwind, Shadcn): Beautiful commercial-grade UX, but high complexity: Node/NPM build chains, state duplication between Python and TypeScript, hydration bugs, and double the maintenance.

PyDataUI eliminates this trade-off.

It provides: - Server-Side Rendering (SSR) + HTMX reactive event delegation: Instant sub-15ms HTML updates with zero user JavaScript. - Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui design system: Commercial, production-grade aesthetics out of the box. - Zero-Class Procedural State Hook (state(**defaults)): Eliminates boilerplate state classes. - Native Multi-Target Compilation: The exact same Python code runs as: - Production Web Application (FastAPI SSR) - Headless GPU / SSH Dashboard (Rich Terminal TUI) - Native Desktop App (Tauri 2.0) - Mobile App / Simulator (Capacitor / PWA)

docs.title: ⚠️ The 5 Anti-Patterns & Learning Curve Traps
docs.text: When developers transition from React or older frameworks, they often write awkward, high-friction Python code. Here is how to avoid the most common traps:

docs.title: 1. The on_change Two-Way Binding Trap
docs.text:
• Anti-Pattern: Attaching an on_change listener to every Input or TextArea to manually sync state.
  • PyDataUI Way: In SSR and HTMX, forms and event handlers pass input values directly into the action arguments: 
    @s.action
def submit_query(message: str = ""):
    s.response = f"Echo: {message}"

docs.title: 2. The children=[...] Keyword Nesting Trap
docs.text:
• Anti-Pattern: Passing lists to children=[...] like Flutter/React.
  • PyDataUI Way: Components accept variable positional arguments *children: 
    # Clean & Pythonic
Card(
    Heading("Overview", level=2),
    Text("Welcome to the operations center."),
    title="System Status"
)

docs.title: 3. Static Class State Ceremony
docs.text:
• Anti-Pattern: Creating class MyState(State): with explicit getters and setters for small tools or scripts.
  • PyDataUI Way: Use the zero-class procedural state hook s = state(**defaults) with @s.action.

docs.title: 4. Nested Card Chat Anti-Pattern
docs.text:
• Anti-Pattern: Rendering chat messages as stacked generic gray Card components with list comprehensions.
  • PyDataUI Way: Use the high-level Chat macro primitive, which automatically renders commercial chat bubbles, avatar indicators, auto-scroll, and Enter-key sending.

docs.title: 5. Fragmenting Web and Terminal Logic
docs.text:
• Anti-Pattern: Writing separate scripts for Web (app.py) and Terminal (cli.py).
  • PyDataUI Way: Write one app. Run it in the browser with pydataui run app.py or in the terminal with pydataui tui app.py.

docs.title: 💬 Pattern: Production-Grade AI Customer Support Chat
docs.text:
Here is the recommended production architecture for building LLM chatbots and agent support consoles:

from pydataui import App, state, Container
from pydataui.components import Chat
import httpx

app = App(title="AI Customer Support")

# 1. Zero-Class Reactive State
s = state(
    messages=[
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "Hello! I am your AI Support Assistant. Ask me anything."}
    ],
    session_id="sess_001",
)

# 2. Asynchronous Message Dispatcher
@s.action
async def handle_chat(message: str = "", **kwargs):
    user_msg = message or kwargs.get("message", "").strip()
    if not user_msg:
        return

    # Instantly reflect user message in conversation
    s.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_msg})

    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000", timeout=120.0) as client:
            resp = await client.post(
                "/chat/invoke",
                json={"id": s.session_id, "message": user_msg}
            )
            resp.raise_for_status()
            reply = resp.json().get("response", "Thank you for reaching out.")
    except Exception as e:
        reply = f"Temporary service notice: {e}"

    # Push assistant response
    s.messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

# 3. Clean Layout
@app.page("/")
def home():
    return Container(
        Chat(
            messages=s.messages,
            title="Customer Support AI",
            placeholder="Type your message and press Enter...",
            on_send=handle_chat,
        ),
        max_width="lg",
        padding="lg",
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=8000)

docs.title: PyDataUI Troubleshooting & Architecture Guide
docs.text: A definitive guide to diagnosing, resolving, and understanding UI responsiveness, reactivity, and distinguishing Framework-Level Issues from Application/Usage-Level Issues.

docs.title: 1. How PyDataUI Reactivity Works
docs.text:
PyDataUI combines Rust Tokio/Hyper (pyrustapi), HTMX (reactive SSR), Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Client Browser                    │
│                                                        │
│  User clicks button or changes input                   │
│  HTMX intercepts event (hx-post, hx-trigger="click")   │
│  Serializes all form inputs via `hx-include="#pdu-root"`│
└──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                           │ HTTP POST /_pdu/event/{State}/{method}
                           │ Body: application/x-www-form-urlencoded / JSON
                           ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   pyrustapi Server Core                │
│                                                        │
│  1. Restores Session from Cookie (`pdu-session`)       │
│  2. Deserializes form fields into State variables      │
│  3. Invokes state method: `State.method(**kwargs)`     │
│  4. Re-renders page fragment: `render_fragment()`      │
│  5. Returns HTML with updated state values (200 OK)    │
└──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                           │ HTTP 200 OK (HTML fragment)
                           ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Client Browser                    │
│                                                        │
│  HTMX swaps `#pdu-root` innerHTML with new HTML       │
│  Tailwind applies updated styles instantaneously       │
│  DOM reflects mutated State without full page reload   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 2. Framework vs. Usage Diagnostic Matrix
docs.text: Symptom Layer Root Cause Resolution DevTools Console: TypeError: Cannot read property of undefined in htmx.min.js Framework Selector missing or invalid target (e.g. closest form when not in <form>). Fixed in v0.2.0: Unified hx-include="#pdu-root". Network Tab: 404 on /_pdu/static/htmx.min.js or .css Framework Static route handler only handling root files or missing MIME type. Fixed in v0.2.0: Streaming response with 18 MIME types and subfolder routing. Black transparent overlay blocks clicks to inputs/buttons Framework Backdrop z-index stacking above modal dialog card. Fixed in v0.2.0: Backdrop at z-index: 1, content strictly at z-index: 10. Server prints HTTP 500 without application traceback Framework Method invocation or page render lacked error boundaries. Fixed in v0.2.0: Error boundaries return #pdu-action-error toast instead of 500. Clicking button does not send any network request Usage Button lacks on_click or called method with parentheses: on_click=State.save() instead of on_click=State.save. Pass method reference: on_click=State.save. Form values are not saved / input value is empty on submit Usage Input missing bind or name: <input> without name cannot be serialized by HTML/HTMX. Add bind=State.my_var or name="my_var". State updates on server but UI displays old data Usage Referenced variable directly my_var instead of State class reference State.my_var. Use Heading(State.count) instead of reading inst.count. Changes not reflected after code edits Usage Running from different Python environment with old PyDataUI package. Ensure pip install -e . is installed in your active Python env.

docs.title: 3. Framework-Level Guarantees (PyDataUI v0.2.0)
docs.text:
1. Zero Client-Side JavaScript Required: Data developers never write JavaScript. All interactivity is declaratively compiled to HTMX attributes.

  2. Self-Healing Error Boundaries: If an exception occurs in your state method (e.g., database connection failure, validation error):

  3. The server never crashes with HTTP 500.
  4. Full traceback is logged to your terminal console.

  5. The UI remains interactive and displays an alert toast banner (#pdu-action-error) on the screen.

  6. Safe Multi-Environment Static Asset Serving: Static assets (htmx.min.js, pydataui.css, SVGs, fonts) are served with StreamingResponse to prevent Rust string-escaping and include CDN fallback onerror handlers.

  7. Descriptor & Falsy Binding Safety: bind=State.field safely retains the descriptor binding even when initial state values are empty strings "", 0, or False.
